    Chapter Notes hello all!

    new chapter for you, and a lot of assassin family content :)

    hope everyone enjoys!

    need to actually write some of this story but have been busy with another project and have been working like crazy these past few weeks.

    have up to chapter 40 written so i've got some weeks before I need to write again tbf but I like to be ahead lol Relief, sharp and sweet, flooded Yelena as she reached the roof hatch once more. The conversation below had been a brutal sucker punch, a dizzying cocktail of revelation and betrayal.

    And Alexei, her supposed father figure, had been tasked with her elimination. Gritting her teeth, Yelena pushed those emotions aside for now. There would be time to deal with the past later. Right now, survival was paramount. She had to get out of this building before anyone discovered a lone Black Widow lurking in the ventilation shafts. The descent down the ladder was swift and silent. Reaching the deserted hallway, Yelena scanned her surroundings. The sterile silence felt suffocating after the low hum of the vents. Following the mental map, she'd pieced together during her crawl, she retraced her steps back to the unguarded access door.

    Outside, the snow continued to fall, blanketing the world in a pristine white. Yelena pulled her stowed away backpack onto hers shoulders. She needed to get to a vantage point, a place where she could observe the building's perimeter and anticipate Alexei's exit. With a practiced eye, she spotted a construction crane looming over the complex, its skeletal frame a perfect lookout point.

    A burst of agility honed by years of training, scaled Yelena up the icy metal beams, her movements swift and silent. The wind whipped at her face, carrying stinging snowflakes, but she barely noticed. Reaching the top platform, she surveyed the scene below. A motorcade of black SUVs was idling near the entrance, a clear sign of an imminent departure. Yelena's pulse quickened. Alexei wouldn't be leaving on foot. Her assumption about Melina's plane was a good one. She just needed to find it.

    A glint on the horizon caught her eye. There, nestled on a secluded helipad, sat a sleek black jet – Melina's pride and joy, a deadly bird painted an innocent black. A triumphant smirk tugged at Yelena's lips. Her ride awaited.

    Now came the tricky part.

    She needed to get to the jet without alerting the waiting security detail. Yelena cast her gaze around, searching for a path, a way to bypass the watchful eyes below. The fire escape provided a tempting route, but the exposed metal would sing its icy song in the frigid night air, drawing unwanted attention.

    Her gaze drifted down the side of the building, the sheer, smooth facade offering no purchase for a traditional climb.

    But Yelena wasn't known for traditional methods.

    A glint of mischief sparked in her eyes. With a silent curse at the added element of risk due to the weather, she started unspooling her trusty length of grappling hook cable from her forearm holster for the second time that day. The metal whispered as it snaked out, the hook glinting more in the pale moonlight than it had in the afternoon sun. Attaching the grappling hook to a sturdy air vent jutting out from the upper floors, she tested the weight with a practiced tug. Satisfied, she gave her usual silent prayer to the engineering gods of whoever built this monstrosity and launched herself over the edge.

    The wind whipped at her face as she descended, the lights of the CIA buildings blurring into streaks of colour below. Her grip tightened on the cable as she rappelled down the slick surface, the friction warming her chilled fingers momentarily. Reaching the halfway point, a sudden gust of wind threatened to send her swinging wildly. Yelena gritted her teeth, adjusting her grip and using the momentum to propel her around the corner of the building. With a practiced manoeuvre, she used her legs to break her descent just before reaching the ground, landing in a crouch behind a large, idling SUV. Her heart hammered against her ribs, a frantic drum solo in the confines of the cramped space. She peeked underneath the vehicle, her eyes scanning the tarmac for any sign of approaching security personnel. Thankfully, the coast was clear. The black behemoths surrounding her cast long, menacing shadows, offering a sliver of cover. Yelena squeezed herself further under the SUV, her backpack mere centimetres off the cold, damp floor as she gripped onto whatever she could find to hold. The strong smell of gasoline and exhaust fumes filled her nostrils, but she barely registered it. Her focus was laser-sharp – reach the jet, confront Alexei, and get out of this frozen hellhole alive.

    Lying there, adrenaline thrumming through her veins, Yelena couldn't help but smirk. Valentina thought she could get rid of her? She thought they could turn her into a ghost? Yelena Belova was a survivor, a weapon honed to a razor's edge.

    Valentina wanted to play this game?

    Game on.

    Headlights flared to life, momentarily blinding her, before the SUV lurched forward, joining the convoy in a slow crawl towards the helipad. Each agonizingly slow second stretched into an eternity. Her cramped quarters were turning into a furnace, the air thick and suffocating. But Yelena held her position, muscles screaming in protest, until the tell-tale dip in the asphalt signalled their arrival at the helipad.

    Peeking out from under the car, Yelena saw the sleek black jet, the unmistakable silhouette, bathed in the harsh glare of landing lights. The other SUVs came to a halt, forming a protective barrier around the aircraft. This was it. Her slim window of opportunity. With a burst of adrenaline, Yelena flung herself out from under the SUV just as the last car in the convoy began to turn away. She rolled onto the tarmac, the rough surface scraping against her exposed skin, before sprinting towards the jet, a dark blur against the snow. A shout pierced the night air, followed by the frantic barks of a security guard dog. But Yelena didn't dare look back. Her focus was singular – the open hatch of the jet, a gaping maw beckoning her in.

    She reached the aircraft mere seconds before the hatch began to close. With a flying leap, born of pure desperation, Yelena launched herself towards the opening, her body twisting in mid-air. Her fingers brushed the metal lip, finding purchase just as the jet started to ascend. With a surge of strength, she pulled herself up, hauling her body through the narrow opening and into the dimly lit cabin.

    The hatch slammed shut behind her with a resounding thud, plunging the interior into near darkness. Yelena landed in a crouch, gasping for breath, her heart a frantic drum solo in her chest. She could hear the receding whine of the security dog, the shouts fading into the distance, just about over the engine’s rumble.

    Yelena's eyes adjusted to the dim light as she rose from her crouched position, her senses on high alert. She scanned her surroundings, taking in the cramped confines of the cargo hold and the crates stacked haphazardly around her.

    "Yelena?" Alexei exclaimed, his voice tinged with disbelief as he turned around at the sound of Yelena’s feet hitting the floor. "What are you doing here?"

    Yelena's lips curved into a cold smirk. "I could ask you the same question, отец," she replied, her tone dripping with disdain. "But I think I already know the answer."

    The small jet touched down with a gentle bump, its sleek form dwarfing the dusty landing strip carved out of the sprawling farmland. Yelena, still buzzing from the adrenaline rush of her surprise entrance, unbuckled herself and cautiously stepped out of the aircraft. Fresh country air, tinged with the earthy scent of damp grass and covered with snow, washed over her, a stark contrast to the sterile air of the CIA headquarters.

    A weathered farmhouse stood in the distance, a beacon of light amidst the vast expanse of darkness. As Yelena descended the metal steps, she heard a furious voice erupt from within the hangar. The language was sharp and Slavic, the fury unmistakable even from this distance.

    "Alexei! You insolent baboon! What in the name of Mother Russia possessed you to take MY plane?!" The voice belonged to a woman, her words laced with a venomous anger that sent shivers down Yelena's spine.

    Yelena peeked around the corner of the hangar, her gaze falling upon a scene straight out of a tense family reunion. Melina, her mother, stood toe-to-toe with Alexei, her face contorted in a mask of rage. Her long black hair, usually worn loose, was pulled back in a tight bun, emphasizing the sharp angles of her face. She was a woman who commanded attention, even in her fury.

    Alexei, on the other hand, looked like a chastised schoolboy caught with his hand in the cookie jar. He shuffled his feet, his shoulders slumped in defeat. "Melina, darling," he stammered, his voice cracking under the pressure of her anger, "it wasn't what you think It was just a little… business trip."

    Melina snorted, a humourless sound devoid of amusement. "Business trip, my backside! Valentin- I told you, Alexei, I specifically said no more involvement with that woman or her… ерунда!!"

    Yelena watched, a silent observer in this expected family drama. So much of what she thought she knew about her past was crumbling around her. Melina, the ruthless Red Room trainer, was also a woman fiercely protective of her own, a woman who defied Valentina. And Alexei, the doting father figure, was a somewhat willing pawn in a deadly game. "Melina, please," Alexei pleaded, his voice laced with desperation. "It wasn't my choice. Valentina… she has leverage. She knows…" He trailed off, his gaze flicking nervously towards Yelena, who remained hidden in the shadows.

    Melina's eyes narrowed, following Alexei's gaze. For a tense moment, their eyes locked, a silent conversation passing between them. Then, Melina's gaze snapped to Yelena, her expression hardening into a mask of icy indifference. A flicker of something else, however, betrayed the steely facade – a flicker of surprise, perhaps even a hint of… relief? Before Yelena could decipher that flicker further, a whirlwind of hair and fury descended upon her. Melina, her anger momentarily forgotten, threw her arms around Yelena in a crushing embrace. The gesture was unexpected, a stark contrast to the cold, distant mother Yelena had always braced herself for.

    "Yelena, moya devochka!” Melina exclaimed, her voice thick with emotion. Yelena stood stiffly, unsure how to respond. Part of her craved this affection, this sense of connection she'd never truly had. But another, more cautious part, held her back. Too many questions swirled in her mind at this moment in time, too many lies had been spun and the whole day had her too wired for the affection from her mother.

    "Melina," Alexei stammered, a touch bewildered by the sudden display of warmth. “Why did I get no hug?” He grumbled.

    Melina ignored him, her focus solely on her daughter. "Come inside, Yelena," she urged, tugging her towards the farmhouse. "You must be freezing after that… whatever ordeal you just endured." Her voice softened as she spoke the last part, a hint of concern peeking through her stern facade.

    Stepping through the farmhouse door, Yelena was hit with a wave of warmth that washed away the chill of the night. The aroma of stewed cabbage and spices filled the air, a familiar comfort from her childhood. The room was sparsely furnished, but a crackling fire blazed in the hearth, casting flickering shadows across the worn armchairs and a large wooden table that dominated the space.

    Yelena's steps faltered in the doorway. Her gaze, drawn by the sound of soft conversation, landed on a figure in the kitchen – Natasha. The blonde had completely forgotten Melina had notified her she was there. Gone were the sleek black suit and confident stance she associated with the Avenger. Natasha was reduced to a simple grey sweatshirt and jeans, stirring a pot perched on a rustic stove. The sight of her, so relaxed and seemingly at home, sent a whirlwind of emotions swirling in Yelena's gut – anger and a flicker of longing. "Yelena! Melina!" Alexei boomed, his voice tinged with relief as he followed them inside, oblivious to the tension radiating off his daughter. “Isn’t this just wonderful?! The whole family back together!"

    Melina, her face unreadable in the flickering firelight, shot Alexei a withering glance. "Yes, Alexei," she said, her voice clipped. "Very nice." Then, with a sigh that spoke volumes of her lingering anger, she turned back to Yelena. "Go get settled in, sweetheart. Your room hasn’t been touched since last time. I'll have some warm food for you in a moment." With a nod, she allowed Melina to shoo her away, the exhaustion of the day leaving her no energy to deal with whatever weird dynamic was about to erupt in the kitchen.

    Natasha watched as Melina ushered Yelena out of the kitchen, before whipping back around into the kitchen, waiting until the door down the hall opened and shut before she turned on Alexei.

    Her eyes narrowed, a dangerous glint replacing the warmth she'd shown Yelena. "Alexei," she hissed, her voice low and menacing, "you had one job. Stay away from Valentina. And what do you do? Steal my plane and create more mess!"

    Alexei, who had been basking in the moment of a seemingly complete family, shrunk back under Melina's glare. His bravado completely deflated; he mumbled a weak apology. "Melina, I… I couldn't help it. Valentina threatened…"

    "Threatened what?" Melina cut him off, her voice dripping with icy contempt. "Don't lie to me, Alexei. You knew what this would do. You knew it would bring Yelena more trouble." "I…" Alexei stammered, searching for an excuse, but Melina wasn't interested in his justifications.

    "Valentina threatened to…" Alexei trailed off, his eyes darting nervously between Melina and Natasha. He knew the weight of his words, the potential fallout if he revealed the truth. But with a deep breath, he steeled himself and blurted out, "She threatened to expose... The past, the identities, the whole damn thing. She has the files. All the files… she could restart the Red Room, just like that." Alexei banged his fist once on his chest, the sound echoing through the quiet kitchen.

    Natasha's blood ran cold. Valentina held all the cards, it seemed.

    Melina, her face a mask of cold fury, slammed a wooden spoon onto the countertop, the clatter echoing like a gunshot in the tense silence. "The Red Room is gone, Alexei. We shut it down years ago." Her voice, though firm, betrayed a sliver of doubt. Years of conditioning weren't easily erased.

    "Or so we thought," Natasha muttered, her voice barely a whisper. Valentina's threat went far beyond mere exposure. It was a challenge, a twisted attempt to reassert control. They had pushed her too far.

    Alexei, sensing the shift in mood, stammered further. "Valentina… she has resources. She knows people. She could find new girls, new Widows, old ones…" His voice trailed off, the horror of the possibility hanging heavy in the air.

    The Red Room, a factory of assassins, churning out emotionless weapons, mixed with the Lufuthai?

    The thought sent chills down Natasha's spine.

    Melina, however, wasn't about to surrender. Her gaze, steely and determined, met Natasha's. "We won't let that happen," she said, her voice carrying the weight of a shared history, of past battles fought and sacrifices made. "We dismantled the Red Room once, and we can do it again, if it comes to it.”

    Melina, for all her faults, was a survivor. She wouldn't back down from a fight, especially one that threatened to drag them all back into the abyss they'd escaped.

    Looking at Melina, her former enemy and reluctant ally, Natasha spoke, her voice laced with newfound resolve. "You need to talk to Yelena. You need to tell her the truth… about everything."

    Melina's eyes narrowed, but a flicker of understanding passed through them. "Yes," she conceded. "She deserves to know." A hint of sadness flickered across her face, a glimpse of a maternal instinct battling years of conditioning.

    The revelation hung heavy in the air. Yelena's arrival, indirectly orchestrated by Valentina, was a clear indicator they were 5 steps behind the Contessa.

    But what was Valentina's ultimate goal?

    Natasha wracked her brain, searching for a pattern, a motive. Kingpin under her thumb, an army of Russian super soldiers and a want for agents in the Red Room program – the pieces didn't quite fit.

    Power?

    Control?

    It seemed too simplistic.

    Natasha's breath hitched.

    A new, more terrifying question arose in the redhead’s mind.

    Was there ever a way to truly escape the Red Room? Was the freedom just an illusion, a fragile construct that could be shattered at any moment by a ghost from the past? Natasha glanced at Melina, a woman haunted by her own choices, and the heavy silence that had descended upon them.

    Natasha couldn't yet fathom, but a shiver ran down her spine nonetheless. The silence didn’t last long for the quiet was shattered with a characteristic lack of subtlety. "So," Alexei boomed, his voice echoing in the tense atmosphere, "what's with all the tension huh? Between you and my little Yelena?” He looked at Natasha as he spoke rather loudly. Natasha winced. Alexei, for all his bluster, possessed the social graces of a bull in a china shop. The last thing she needed right now was his insensitive prodding. Melina shot him a withering glance, but before she could retort, Natasha spoke.

    "It's a long story, Alexei," she said, her voice clipped.

    "Oh, I've got time," he declared, oblivious to the tension he was amplifying. He pulled out a chair and plopped himself down at the table, a wide grin plastered across his face. "I remember when you two were little. Always causing a ruckus! Couldn't be separated for a single minute. Demanded to sleep in the same bed so you wouldn't be apart." A ghost of a smile touched Natasha's lips at the memory. There was a time, before the Red Room had twisted and warped their lives, when she and Yelena had been inseparable. Two little girls, clinging to each other for comfort and security in a world that felt increasingly cold and unforgiving to Natasha. She was glad Yelena had that time to be naïve and unknowing about the actual situation.

    Melina, however, remained unmoved by Alexei's nostalgic ramblings. "Those days are long gone, Alexei," she said, her voice laced with a weariness that belied her years. "The world has changed them both."

    "Well, that's a shame," Alexei said, a frown creasing his brow. He looked at Natasha, his gaze filled with a genuine concern that surprised her. "You two were like sisters once." He hesitated, then added, almost sheepishly, "Always thought you'd end up looking after each other, you know? Taking care of one another."

    The weight of his words hung heavy in the air. Natasha looked away, the past a painful tapestry she wasn't ready to revisit, not with Alexei as the narrator. They were all products of the Red Room, their lives fractured, and their relationships warped. Sisterhood, in the truest sense, was something they'd never truly known, not since that day in Cuba. Alexei's cheerful demeanour faltered at the redheads reaction. He opened his mouth to speak, but Melina cut him off with a raised hand. "There will be time for explanations later," she said firmly. "But right now, we have more pressing matters at hand." Her eyes flickered towards Natasha, a silent plea for her to keep the conversation brief.

    Natasha understood. Melina, unlike Alexei, likely had a deeper understanding of Yelena's anger, perhaps even privy to Yelena’s more nuanced feelings. With a sigh, Natasha offered Alexei a tight smile.

    "Let's just say," she began, choosing her words carefully, "Yelena feels… betrayed. She believes I abandoned her, that I left her alone in that program and that I repeated that when I died on Vormir." It was a gross oversimplification, but for now, it would have to do. Alexei's expression fell. A flicker of guilt clouded over his eyes. "But… you had no choice, did you?" he stammered. "You saved the world. My daughter! And now you’ve returned! Like… like? A Russian Jesus!” The large man exclaimed.

    "That's not the point," Natasha interjected, her voice laced sounding as fed up as she looked. "The point is, she's hurting, and angry and I don’t know how to fix it.” Just then, the creak of the kitchen door sliced through the tension. Yelena stood framed in the doorway, her arms crossed, and a scowl etched on her face. She had changed out of her suit and into comfy clothes that she left here last time. Her blonde hair was wavy and wet hanging down her shoulders. The air crackled with unspoken words and years of resentment. Natasha felt a pang of something akin to hope. Perhaps, a conversation, however difficult, was better than this heavy silence. She opened her mouth to speak, but Yelena cut her off. "You don't," Yelena said, her voice clipped and cold. Her gaze flicked from Natasha to Melina, then settled back on Natasha with a burning intensity. "You don't know how to fix anything. You just… disappear.

    The words were like a punch to the gut. Natasha managed to hold back the flinch that tried to escape her at the words.

    "Yelena," Melina began, her voice firm but laced with a hint of maternal concern. "There's a lot we need to talk about…"

    "Is there?" Yelena interrupted, her voice dripping with sarcasm. "Because from where I'm standing, it seems like you've all been doing a pretty good job of talking without me. Years I spent…" Her voice trailed off, her jaw clenching as she fought back a wave of emotion. Natasha watched her, her heart heavy. Yelena's anger was raw and justified, a reflection of the pain they'd both endured. The redhead didn’t miss the flicker of vulnerability, a longing for a connection that had been severed, sweep across the blonde’s face. Perhaps, Natasha thought, there was still a chance to bridge the gap, to rebuild the trust that had been shattered. "Years I spent… being poked and prodded, turned into a weapon! While you two… what? Lived normal lives? Had pig families? Got to be heroes?” Yelena started again, her focus on Melina and Natasha, ignoring Alexei who was not so subtly slipping out of the back door, snagging a box of cereal off the side as he went.

    "No," Natasha said, her voice thick with emotion. "It wasn't like that. I never forgot about you, Yelena. Never a single day." But the words rang hollow, even to her own ears. How could she explain the years of silence, the buried memories, the life she'd built for herself while Yelena remained trapped?

    Yelena scoffed, a harsh, humourless sound.

    The room held its breath as Yelena's raw emotions filled the space.

    "Yelena," Melina said, her voice firm but laced with an understanding tone that Natasha could never quite muster. "We know this is difficult. We understand your anger, your hurt." A flicker of pain crossed Melina's own face, a silent acknowledgment of her own role in the past.

    "Difficult?" Yelena spat, her voice tight. "You have no idea. Years of chemicals entering my body, of being turned into a mindless weapon! And all the while, you…" She gestured towards Natasha, her blue eyes blazing with a mixture of fury and despair. "You were out there, living a life! Free."

    Natasha flinched this time, the searing truth knocking her backward. Melina, however, met Yelena's gaze head-on. "No, Yelena," she countered gently. "Natasha's life wasn't a walk in the park. She escaped the Red Room, yes, but the scars run deep. She carries the burden of what happened every single day."

    Yelena scoffed, but a flicker of doubt flickered in her eyes. Melina, sensing a shift, pressed on. "Look," she said, her voice softening further. "We both failed you, Yelena. We failed to protect you, to shield you from the horrors of the Red Room. But that doesn't mean we don't care."

    The word "care" hung heavy in the air. Yelena remained silent, her gaze locked on Melina, searching for any hint of insincerity. A muscle in her jaw clenched and unclenched, betraying the storm of emotions churning beneath the surface. Her day, already a tangled mess, felt suffocatingly heavy under the weight of Melina's words.

    "Care?" Yelena finally spat; the word laced with venom. "You decide to care now? After all these years, after I spent the better part of my life a prisoner in that damn program and in my own head. Where was this care when I needed it most?" Her voice cracked on the last word, a flicker of vulnerability breaking through the facade of anger.

    The years of isolation, the relentless training, the constant fear – it all came flooding back, a torrent of pain that threatened to drown her. Natasha watched, her heart twisting in her chest. Melina, for all her attempts at understanding, couldn't erase the past. Couldn't undo the damage.

    "Yelena, we…" Melina began, her voice softening with genuine regret. But Yelena cut her off.

    "We what?" Yelena challenged, her voice rising. "We get to live our lives while I rotted in that place? We get happy endings while mine was ripped away?" Her gaze darted between Natasha and Melina, the accusation in her eyes clear. "It doesn't do me much good now, does it? All this talk of caring, of understanding. It doesn't bring back the years I lost. It doesn't erase the things they did to me. The things you did to me." The blonde glared down her mother.

    A fresh wave of anger, hotter and more volatile than before, washed over Yelena. For the past few months, she'd thought, naively perhaps, that she’d reached some kind of understanding with her mother. They'd talked, they'd shared a tentative bond over their shared past at the Red Room, even had a normal mother/daughter relationship.

    But seeing Natasha here reignited the embers of resentment.

    Yelena took a deep breath, forcing herself to calm down. The anger was a familiar friend, but it wouldn't solve anything. “Look, Melina," she said, her voice thick with emotion, "I know you didn't have a choice. We both did what we had to do to survive. We talked about this already, remember? I get it. It doesn't mean I have to like it, but I get it." She reached out and squeezed her mother's hand, a gesture of grudging understanding and her want to continue their tentative relationship as they had been.

    Melina squeezed back, her eyes watery looking at her youngest daughter. Natasha, sensing the shift in Yelena's mood, stepped forward, chancing her luck. "Yelena, I know it's not simple," she interjected gently. “But maybe, just maybe, we can try to move past everything. Like you and Melina seem to be doing." She gestured towards Melina, a flicker of hope flickering in her eyes. "Can we try, for each other?"

    Yelena scoffed. "Spare me the hero's monologue, Nat.”

    “I-I wasn-“ Natasha started to defend herself.

    “Time.” The blonde exhaled slowly, the air escaping her lungs in a sigh more than anything. “What?”

    Defeat tinged her voice as she spoke, barely a whisper. "Time," she echoed, the word hanging heavy in the air like a lead weight. “I need time. And a lot of it.”

    A flicker of relief washed over Natasha. It wasn't a perfect solution, but it was a start. A fragile truce had been reached, and for now, that was enough for the redhead.

    The fragrant aroma of pepperoni and melted cheese hung heavy in the air as Kate Bishop clattered through the door of her loft apartment, a triumphant grin plastered across her face. Behind her, trailed a reluctant Sonya with a sigh that could have curdled milk. "Welcome to my humble abode!” Kate announced with a theatrical flourish, gesturing grandly towards the sparsely furnished living space. A single, lumpy couch sat defiantly in the centre of the room, surrounded by haphazardly stacked pizza boxes and movie posters plastered on the exposed brick walls.

    Sonya bypassed the theatrics and made a beeline for the small kitchen tucked into the corner. She scanned the refrigerator, its contents limited to half a carton of expired yogurt and a jar of questionable-looking pickles.

    "Charming décor, Bishop," Sonya deadpanned, grabbing a bottle of water from the near- empty fridge. "Though it seems your culinary skills haven't improved much since Yelena told me about your lack of cutlery."

    Kate, unfazed by the jab, plopped down on the couch with a dramatic sigh. "Hey, cut a girl some slack! I've been busy avoiding getting murdered remember? Besides, takeout is practically a national pastime in New York."

    Sonya took a long pull from her water bottle, eyeing Kate with amusement. For all her bluster, there was a genuine warmth in Kate's eyes that put Sonya at ease. She could see why Yelena was so fond of the young woman.

    "So," Kate continued, her voice bouncing off the bare walls, "how about a celebratory pizza to mark my triumphant return? My treat, since you so graciously agreed to escort me on this little… retrieval mission."

    Sonya raised an eyebrow. "Celebratory? The only thing we retrieved was a massive headache from the overwhelming smell of cheese downstairs and a reminder of just how дерьмо you are in the kitchen.”

    A shadow flickered across Kate's face for a brief moment, but it was quickly replaced by her usual bravado. "Hey, who knows? Maybe Laura will teach me to cook over Christmas?” "That is not how Laura Barton should be spending the holidays," Sonya said, a hint of amusement dancing in her eyes. "I am sure that is not a relaxing situation or an enjoyable one." Her smirk widened, pushing Kate's buttons with practiced ease.

    Kate rolled her eyes, a playful retort forming on her lips. "So," Kate began hesitantly, her voice softer than Sonya was accustomed to, "have you heard from Yelena? Will she be at the Barton's for Christmas?"

    Sonya, surprised by the unexpected question, hesitated for a moment. The truth was, she hadn't spoken to Yelena since their exchange on the phone and that was about 4 days ago. The blonde could be dead in the middle of nowhere Langley for all she knew. "I… I'm not sure," Sonya admitted, her voice carefully neutral. “It will depend on her, I suppose."

    "Speaking of…" Kate began, a mischievous glint in her eyes, "are you coming to the Bartons' for Christmas?"

    Sonya raised an eyebrow, a faint smile playing on her lips. Laura Barton, with her gentle demeanour and unwavering kindness, had extended the invitation, but Sonya had politely declined.

    "Actually," Sonya replied, "I believe I'll be spending the holidays with some of the other Widows. We may not have had much of a traditional upbringing, but we're trying to create some new traditions of our own."

    Kate's expression softened. "New traditions, huh?" Kate said, a thoughtful look on her face. "Well, hey, maybe next year you can all come celebrate at the Barton farm! We could have a big Widow-Hawkeye holiday extravaganza!"

    The image of Natasha Romanoff, Yelena Belova, and a dozen other Black Widows mingling awkwardly with Clint Barton amidst a sea of Christmas decorations was a bizarre one, but a smile bloomed on Sonya's face nonetheless.

    "An extravaganza, huh?" Sonya said, her voice laced with amusement. "We'll see about that, Bishop. But for now, how about we focus on getting you back to the farm and out of this… culinary wasteland?"

    Kate grinned, a playful glint back in her eyes. "Deal. But only after I order that celebratory pizza… oh and we have to go see the tree… at the Rockefeller. It’s tradition.” Sonya snorted, "Tradition, Bishop? You haven't even lived long enough to establish a tradition for making toast in the morning, let alone visiting a giant, overpriced Christmas tree."

    Kate's smile faltered slightly, a hint of wounded pride flickering across her face. "Hey! It's a New York City tradition! Everyone goes to see the tree at Rockefeller Centre. It's practically mandatory for residents. Yelena saw it… on the floor… but she saw it." Sonya raised an eyebrow sceptically but with a hint of amusement. "Mandatory, huh? Sounds like government overreach to me. Sightseeing seems a tad… irresponsible, when a lot of people would love to have your head on a stick Kate. But hey, at least Yelena got the full New York experience last year, though right? It's not every day you get to witness someone admiring the majestic wonder of a tree from such a unique perspective," she remarked with a playful wink.

    Kate crossed her arms, a playful pout forming on her lips. She knew Sonya wouldn't be swayed by a little holiday cheer, but she couldn't resist trying. "Aw, come on. What's the worst that could happen? We grab a slice of overpriced pizza from a street vendor, admire the sparkly lights for ten minutes, and then I teleport us back here with Lucky the Pizza Dog in tow. Quick in and out, minimal risk, maximum holiday spirit."

    Sonya couldn't help a smile tugging at the corner of her lips. Kate's enthusiasm, infectious as ever, was a welcome change from the grim realities they usually faced. But the woman’s safety remained a priority.

    "Lucky the Pizza Dog, huh?" Sonya said, a hint of amusement in her voice. "And where exactly is this canine companion of yours?"

    Kate's shoulders slumped slightly. "Oh, right," she mumbled, sheepishly rubbing the back of her neck. "Laura’s still babysitting him at the farm. Guess the teleporting with a dog plan is out the window."

    Sonya chuckled, the tension easing from her shoulders. "Perhaps your tradition will have to wait for another year, Bishop.” She gestured towards the phone in Kate's hand. "Pizza first, then we get you back to the Barton farm and prepare for whatever mess awaits us in the new year.”

    Kate sighed dramatically, but a smile lingered on her face. "Fine, fine," she conceded, pulling up a pizza delivery app on her phone. "But next year, Rockefeller Centre, no arguments!" A sudden, sharp rap against the window sent Kate's phone clattering to the floor. Both women whirled around, Sonya’s hands instinctively flying to her weapons. Sonya drew her pistol with lightning speed, aiming it at the source of the sound. Kate’s heart hammered in her chest, adrenaline flooding her system. An ambush? Here?

    Through the grime-coated windowpane, a face materialized. Not an enemy combatant, but one that sent a jolt of surprise through the pair, nonetheless. Yelena Belova stood outside; her expression unreadable in the dim light filtering in from the streetlamps below. Kate's gasp echoed in the room, shattering the tense silence. All thoughts of pizza and playful banter vanished, replaced by a mixture of shock and wary curiosity.

    "Yelena?" Kate breathed, her voice barely a whisper.

    The brunette hurried over to the window and threw it open. She stepped back, creating space for Yelena to climb inside. Yelena clambered through the window with a practiced ease, her movements ingrained in her muscle memory.

    "О, тогда ты не умер," Sonya greeted with a hint of amusement, holstering her weapon, "Хорошо знать."

    “Ты думал, что я умер? Ха. Нет, я слишком хорош для этого.” Yelena laughs, the amusement not quite reaching her eyes, but the noise came out none the less. “Неужели дела пошли настолько плохо?” Sonya asked, having noticed the weight that sat on the blonde’s shoulders.

    “Я объясню позже.” Yelena brushed off Sonya’s concern as the other widow threw the half empty water bottle to the blonde who caught it, nodding gratefully, before taking a sip. “Конечно. Я забыл, что у тебя есть важные дела. Тогда давай, поздоровайся со своей девушкой.” Sonya smirked, her eyes glittering and her smile blinding.

    Kate's interruption broke the glare the blonde was aiming at Sonya, drawing Yelena's attention away from the other widow. "Hello? I'm still here… and I still don't speak Russian?" The brunette interjected, her voice laced with mild exasperation. Sonya's laughter filled the air as she leaned closer to Yelena, speaking in Russian. "Ты видишь, какая она? Кэйт тут бегает, как потерянный щенок, когда тебя нет," she remarked, her tone teasing but affectionate.

    Yelena couldn't help but smirk at Sonya's comment, a playful glint in her eyes. "Спасибо, Соня," she replied in Russian, her lips quirking up into a smile. “You are relieved of your duties. Have a nice Christmas.”

    Kate crossed her arms, a mock offended expression on her face as she looked between the two widows. "Hey, I may not be able to understand a word you’re saying but I can understand the tone, you know," she teased in English, her lips curling into a playful grin. "I'm not that clueless."

    Sonya laughed, patting Kate's shoulder. "Don't worry, sweetheart," she said with a wink. "Nothing you need to be concerned about."

    "Ну же, поприветствуй свою подругу," Sonya then urged having turned back to Yelena, her voice laced with amusement.

    “Почему ты все еще здесь?” Yelena questioned, the small smile on the blonde’s face giving away that she knew exactly why Sonya was still there.

    “Ну давай же. Пошутите меня. Обнимите ее. Это не будет первым.” Sonya winked, wiggling her shoulders in a weird shimmy of excitement. The movement getting even more rapid when Yelena actually groaned out loud, her eyes flicking to the bundle of vibrating energy that was Kate across the room.

    “Я больше никогда не оставлю тебя с ней наедине.” Yelena sighed, titling her head back in her exasperation as Sonya laughed so loudly it took her oldest friend by surprise. “Клянусь Богом, Елена. Обнимите бедную девочку.” Sonya’s face morphed into deadly serious in a split second.

    “Guys?” Kate's voice emerged amidst the rapid-fire Russian, a hint of playful annoyance lacing her tone. “Still here…”

    “Идти.” Sonya said at Yelena clapping her on the shoulder with a wink, before turning to Kate with a wide smile. “We know little hawk. Yelena will come say hello when she’s mustered the courage.”

    Yelena scowled playfully at Sonya, her cheeks burning a faint pink. She shot Sonya a withering look that spoke volumes about her desire for her to leave. With a resigned sigh, Yelena crossed the gap between herself and Kate. She wasn't one for big and obvious displays of affection, especially in front of Sonya of all people, but upon reaching Kate, Yelena hesitated for a fraction of a second, and her mind said Sonya be damned. The blonde surprised them all by throwing her arms around Kate in a tight embrace. Kate, speechless for a moment, froze in surprise. This wasn't the greeting she'd expected from Yelena, especially after how they left things and with Sonya in the room. Slowly, Kate's initial shock melted away, replaced by a warmth that spread through her chest. She tentatively wrapped her arms around Yelena's back, a hesitant smile gracing her lips. This unexpected hug, a silent apology, and a hesitant step towards the promise of something new blooming between them.

    Sonya couldn't help but smirk as she watched the scene unfold before her, her eyes gleaming mischievously as she wiggled her eyebrows at Kate. As Kate hugged Yelena back, a hesitant smile tugging at her lips, Sonya's grin widened. It was a small victory, but a victory, nonetheless. Plus, it was sweet watching her supposed cold-hearted friend become all gooey over a dorky little archer like Kate Bishop.

    Sonya couldn't resist the urge to interject. With a smirk playing on her lips, she cleared her throat to get their attention, relishing in the sight of their tentative embrace. "Alright lovebirds, as much as I'd love to stay and witness the blossoming romance, duty calls," Sonya teased, her tone light but tinged with affection. "Have a good Christmas at the Bartons', you two. Try not to set anything on fire."

    Yelena opened her mouth to protest, pulling away from Kate, but Sonya shot her a warning glare that silenced her objections before they could even form. The message was clear, and Yelena shouldn’t argue with it.

    "But Natasha is already there," Yelena argued anyways, her voice tinged with frustration. "We'll fight, ruin Christmas—"

    Sonya cut her off with a dismissive wave of her hand. "Trust me, if anyone can handle you two, it's Laura and Clint. Now go, have fun, поцелуй ястреба под омелой, and try not to kill your sister."

    Yelena rolled her eyes at Sonya's comment, her annoyance evident in the way she crossed her arms tightly over her chest. "Fine," she muttered begrudgingly, though a small smirk played at the corner of her lips. "But only because you're so insistent, Sonya." With a huff, she turned away from the departing widow and grabbed Kate's hand. "Come on, Kate. Let's go spread some Christmas cheer, or whatever."

    Kate grinned, squeezing the hand in hers.

    As they headed towards the front door, following after Sonya, Yelena couldn't help but mutter under her breath, "поцелуй ястреба под омелой, my ass."

    The Quinjet's sleek belly glinted under the lights as Yelena and Kate Bishop walked down to the main compound hangar. Laughter trailed behind them, muffled by the heavy metal door as they entered.

    "Alright, that's all my stuff." Kate declared, dumping a duffel bag overflowing with clothes onto a nearby table.

    Yelena scanned the room, a flicker of something crossing her features. There, leaning casually against a weapons rack, stood Clint Barton. He was dressed for the cold, a thick coat zipped up over a worn S.H.I.E.L.D. vest. Beside him, a mountain of mismatched bags cast a long shadow across the hangar floor.

    "Barton?" Yelena's voice echoed in the large space.

    Clint's head snapped up, a grin splitting his face. "Yelena! Welcome back! Didn't expect to see you tonight.” His grin faltered when his brow raised in question. "Where's Sonya?" "She’s gone back to Russia to spend the holiday with the other widows.” Clint's surprise softened into understanding. "Ah, of course. Makes sense." He clapped his hands together, his usual cheer returning. "Well, no time to waste then! We gotta get you two to Bartons' Farm, stat! Christmas isn't gonna wait." Before Yelena could protest, Clint was already ushering them towards the Quinjet, his arm slung around Kate's shoulders. "Come on, come on, let's get this holiday party started!"

    “Where did all your holiday cheer come from old man?” Kate questioned from under his arm as they made their way into the cabin, Yelena wasting no time to take control of the flight deck, much to Clint’s displeasure if the look on his face was anything to go by. A mock scowl crossed Clint's features. "Hey! Show some respect for your elders, especially the ones who are bringing you home for Christmas dinner." He winked at Kate. "I enjoy the holidays kid, even more so when I’m not dodging assassination attempts days before.” Yelena's laugh cut through the air as she flipped switches and initiated the pre-flight sequence. “Facing off against powered-up weirdos isn't exactly the worst way to spend a December. I'm not apologizing for it.”

    Clint raised an eyebrow. "Some holiday tradition, huh? You got any more of those?" Yelena smirked. "Let's just say I'm impartial to a good winter hunt. Especially when the prey wears fancy tights and shoots glowing arrows."

    Clint chuckled, shaking his head. He couldn't help but smile at their banter. Still, a nagging question lingered in the back of his mind. He glanced at Yelena, his smile turning a touch softer. "Yelena, listen," he began cautiously, "This is great, you coming for Christmas. But if the missi-…” He trailed off, not wanting to pry, but also genuinely concerned. Yelena seemed to sense his unspoken question. Her usual sharp demeanour softened a touch. "Things are...complicated," she admitted, her voice low. "Let’s just focus on getting to that farm and some decent food, alright?” The blonde muttered under her breath, keeping her voice down so Kate who was further down the cabin couldn’t hear.

    “Yelena… we can’t help if we aren’t clued in.”

    “Has it occurred to you that I don’t want your help? That I don’t need your help?” The assassin semi-growled, stopping herself as Kate wandered back their way, resting her arms on the back of Yelena’s chair.

    Clint went to open his mouth again but Yelena cut him off with a light wave. "We'll talk later Barton. Right now, buckle up, grumpy grandpa. Time to get this reindeer on the road...err, I mean, Quinjet in the air."

    Despite the playful face Yelena had plastered on at Kate’s return, Clint couldn't help but notice a flicker of something in her eyes - a hint of worry beneath the usual bravado. It was a fleeting glimpse, easily missed by anyone who didn't know widows like he did. Years of covert ops with Natasha had made him adept at reading people, especially those skilled at hiding their true feelings.

    Yelena's sudden arrival, on top of Sonya's fleeting exit, sent a knot of unease tightening in Clint's gut. The mission, whatever it was, clearly hadn't gone according to the blonde’s plan. He knew Yelena wouldn't back down from a fight, but the tightness in her jaw and the forced cheer in her voice spoke volumes. There was a story there, one she wasn't ready to share just yet.

    Part of him wanted to press, to offer a listening ear and another person of support for his best friends little sister. But another part, a more cautious, knowledgeable one, recognized the need for space. Yelena, for all her newfound openness, still carried the ingrained secrecy of a Widow's training.

    Pushing her wouldn't help.

    He settled for planning a different approach. A warm, welcoming environment at the farm, good food, and maybe even a snowball fight (though knowing Yelena, it would quickly turn into a competitive display of tactical manoeuvres). Perhaps surrounded by the warmth of his family and the quiet beauty of a winter landscape, similar to one of Russia, Yelena might feel comfortable enough to open up.

    In the meantime, Clint couldn't shake the feeling that he owed it to Natasha, to their shared past, to be there for Yelena. He might not know her little sister as well as he wished, but he understood the weight of loss and the burden of grief that Nat had placed on both of them when she made her decision. Clint also understood the anger Yelena felt but the archer didn’t have it in him to bear that rage, he was too overjoyed with Nat’s return to be wasting all that time and energy being mad at her.

    The whine of the Quinjet throttled down to a low growl as Yelena expertly guided it through a narrow pathway, sunlight filtering through the snowfall, painting the clouds in hues of orange and pink. Finally, with a gentle bump, the aircraft settled onto a hidden landing pad nestled amidst a clearing in the woods.

    Clint unbuckled, a wave of nostalgia washing over him. This secluded landing zone had been a favourite tactic of his and Natasha's during their S.H.I.E.L.D. days. He glanced towards Yelena, her features unreadable in the fading light, the worry in her eyes seemed even more pronounced.

    "Ready to face the Barton family onslaught?" Clint asked with a light nudge to Kate as he tore his eyes from the blonde, who was throwing bag after bag on her back, making her look like a pack mule more than a deadly assassin.

    Kate offered a beaming smile, "Can’t wait.”

    With their bags slung over their shoulders, they stepped out of the Quinjet. The crisp night air hit them like a slap, laden with the scent of pine and woodsmoke. Snow crunched under their boots as they trekked through the silent woods, the only sound their own quiet breaths and the distant hoot of an owl.

    After what felt like an eternity, a warm glow pierced through the darkness. As they drew closer, the unmistakable outline of the Barton farmhouse emerged, its windows ablaze with golden light. A plume of fragrant smoke curled from the chimney, promising warmth and comfort.

    Before they could even reach the porch, the door creaked open, revealing a smiling Laura Barton.

    "You made it!" Laura's voice rang out, warm and welcoming. Her gaze flicked to Kate and Yelena behind her husband, a questioning smile playing on her lips for just a moment before Clint gave her a look. "Hi Kate honey, Yelena. Come in, come in, you both must be freezing!"

    Without another word, Laura ushered them inside, the wave of heat and the sound of quiet Christmas music washing over them like a comforting blanket. Clint couldn't help but grin. Maybe, just maybe, this Christmas wouldn't be so bad after all.

    "The kids and Nat are already tucked in, besides Coop who is probably awake," Laura announced, her voice laced with amusement. "So, you don't have to worry about being bombarded by all that energy tonight." A flicker of relief crossed Yelena’s face, while Clint let out a groan that could only be described as blissful.

    "Sleep for a year, sounds about right," Clint muttered, collapsing gratefully into a nearby armchair.

    Laura chuckled, the sound like wind chimes on a crisp day. "Don't tempt fate, Hawkeye. You know you wouldn't last a week without talking to those kids." She reached over and ruffled his hair affectionately. "Shove off upstairs. I'll bring you up a cup of tea in a moment." Clint shot Kate and Yelena a teasing grin. "See, Barton hospitality at its finest. A warm bed and a scolding." He lumbered to his feet, muscles protesting after the flight. Laura turned to Kate, a warm smile on her face. "There are fresh sheets on your bed, sweetheart. Take your bags upstairs and get settled in."

    Kate nodded, her eyes flitting between Laura and Yelena. The brunette’s gaze lingered on Yelena, titling her head slightly toward the stairs. This Christmas gathering was unexpected given everything going on, and Kate, ever perceptive, picked up on the undercurrent of tension beneath the surface. Yelena, for all her attempts at normalcy, seemed a little…off. Yelena just smiled with a shake of her head, indicating to Kate to go on without her. The smile, however, didn't quite reach her eyes.

    With a hesitant nod, Kate slung her bag over her shoulder and started towards the stairs. But not before shooting one last confused look back at Yelena and Laura. The unspoken question hung in the air – was everything alright with Yelena?

    Laura, ever the diplomat, simply offered another reassuring smile and a gentle nudge towards the stairs. "Go on, get comfy, dear. Yelena will be fine with me, I don’t bite.” The woman teased with a small grin.

    Kate, with one final glance, reluctantly climbed the stairs, her curiosity piqued. Yelena watched Kate's back until it disappeared around the corner at the top of the stairs, the pitter-patter of her footsteps fading into the background. Then, she let out a long, slow exhale, the weight of the past couple days finally pressing down on her. With a tired sigh, she pushed herself away from the wall and leaned back onto the kitchen countertop across from Laura, who was expertly measuring tea leaves into a steaming mug. The fragrant steam danced upwards, carrying a welcome warmth.

    "Anything I can get you, Yelena?" Laura asked, her voice soft and knowing. Her gaze held a quiet understanding that went beyond words. Years of friendship with Natasha had honed Laura's intuition, and she could see the turmoil simmering beneath Yelena's stoic facade. "If you could get my life to start over, without the Red Room, that'd be great." The blonde said with a deadpan tone, her eyes droopy and face gaunt.

    Laura chuckled softly, the sound warm and genuine. "Well, a fresh start might be out of my reach," she admitted, her gaze softening further. "I wish I could, honey. I'd give anything for you and Natasha not to have experienced what you had to." A shadow of grief flickered across her face, a silent acknowledgement of the amount of pain their little group bore between them.

    Laura's words were simple, yet laced with a sincerity that resonated with Yelena. The dam holding back her emotions threatened to burst. Yelena clenched her jaw, forcing her breaths to come out in measured gasps, willing the tears back. Focus on the warmth, she told herself. Focus on the smell of the tea and remember the smell of the pine outside. Focus on Laura's gentle presence.

    Laura understood. She gave Yelena a moment, turning back to the straining tea leaves before turning back to the blonde. Her voice was quiet, filled with an unwavering support. "What happened, Yelena?" she asked, the question hanging in the air, a safe harbour for the storm brewing within the young woman.

    Yelena stared into the swirling vortex of the teacup on the side, the silence stretching between them. Finally, the blonde spoke, her voice barely a whisper. "It's…complicated. And for now," she continued, her gaze flickering up to meet Laura's with a steely glint, "it's safer for everyone if I'm the only one who knows.”

    Laura's brow furrowed in concern. "Safer for everyone?" she echoed, her voice gentle but firm. "Yelena, honey, you going at it alone isn't safer. You deserve to have someone you can trust, to lean on."

    Yelena's jaw clenched for a moment, then she sighed, a wave of weariness washing over her. "I know," she admitted, her voice barely a rasp. "But trust me, Laura, in this case, silence really is golden. This...situation, it’s... the fewer people who know the details, the better." A flicker of worry crossed Laura's eyes. "Does Natasha know?"

    Yelena shook her head, the movement small and almost imperceptible. "No. Just me and Alexei."

    Her voice held a hint of something Laura couldn't quite place, a mixture of fear and a strange protectiveness.

    "Alexei?" Laura echoed, a beat of surprise in her voice. "But I thought..." She trailed off, unsure if she should pry further.

    Yelena seemed to sense her hesitation. "It's a long story," the assassin said, her gaze flickering towards the stairs.

    "Alright, dear," Laura said gently, placing a steaming mug in front of Yelena. "Take your time. And remember, Clint and I are here for you, no matter what. Always." Yelena offered a small, grateful smile. Picking up the mug, she took a tentative sip, the warmth spreading through her chilled fingers.

    Laura lingered for a moment, her gaze holding Yelena's. "You know, honey," she said softly, "if you ever do want to talk, I have all the time in the world."

    Yelena shook her head, a flicker of something akin to gratitude flitting across her eyes. "Thank you, Laura. I think I just need some quiet." She forced a smile, a hint of hope peeking through. "Maybe later, after some sleep. We can swap stories about the worst missions we've ever been on. Deal?"

    Laura chuckled, the sound warm and genuine. "Sounds like a plan. In the meantime," she said, picking up Clint's forgotten tea, she gestured towards the stairs. "the dogs are down in the basement with Cooper, who's probably still glued to his Xbox. But if you need anything at all, don't hesitate to come and ask."

    Yelena nodded her acknowledgement, a ghost of a smile playing on her lips. As Laura disappeared up the stairs, the farmhouse settling into a comfortable silence, Yelena flopped down onto the sofa, the mug warming her hands. Taking a deep breath, she closed her eyes, the weight of her secrets momentarily overshadowed by the promise of a warm fire, a steaming cup of tea, and the unexpected comfort of Laura Barton.

    But the respite was short-lived. As soon as her eyelids fluttered shut, her mind kicked back into overdrive. Kingpin. A tangled web of deceit and manipulation. Kate, caught in the crosshairs, oblivious to the level of danger she was in. Valentina, a ghost from the past, resurfacing with an agenda Yelena couldn't decipher. And then there was the whole Alexei situation. What purpose did he serve? Was he a pawn, or a player in this deadly game? Maybe we should’ve thrown him back in prison.

    Yelena winced, the warmth of the teacup a stark contrast to the icy fear that coiled in her gut. Most of all, there was Natasha. The thought of her sister, her person, brought a lump to Yelena's throat. How much did Natasha know? Did Alexei tell her? Was she in danger too? The largest question still bothering her was, how did Natasha come back from the dead in the first place?

    And then there was Kate.

    Yelena sighed, the sound a mix of exasperation and something strangely tender. The woman was a walking contradiction – an archer with a heart of gold, a clumsy goofball who possessed a razor-sharp mind. Yelena found herself strangely drawn to Kate's infectious energy, her unwavering want to see the good in everyone, including Yelena herself. It was a stark contrast to the cynicism Yelena had cultivated over the years, a shield against the harsh realities of her life. Kate was younger, less jaded. She saw the good in the world, a naïveté that both annoyed and endeared Yelena.

    However, that very naïveté was Kate’s biggest downfall. Yelena knew the darkness that lurked beneath the surface of everyone, no one is truly good, the dangers that could consume someone whole are just waiting to be prodded, and the head always rears at some point. Valentina wouldn’t hesitate to use Kate and Kingpin wouldn't hesitate to kill her, and Yelena was desperate to keep her out of harm’s way.

    A frustrated laugh escaped Yelena's lips. Keeping Kate safe, however, was easier said than done. The woman had a stubborn streak a mile wide, one that could even rival the blonde’s own. Telling her everything, dumping the weight of the situation on her shoulders, felt almost cruel. Would Kate believe the depths of the conspiracy, the danger that loomed? Or would she charge headfirst into the fray, without thinking like she always does? Yelena traced the rim of her teacup with a finger, the condensation leaving a cool trail. The answer, she realized, wasn't clear-cut. Maybe there was a middle ground, a way to protect Kate without robbing her of her agency.

    But how could Yelena protect them both, when she felt like she was drowning in a sea of secrets?

    She squeezed her eyes shut tighter, willing the questions to recede. They persisted, a relentless chorus in the quiet of the farmhouse. Sleep, for now, seemed like an impossible dream. Instead, Yelena found herself lost in a mental labyrinth, desperately searching for a way out, a way to keep Kate safe, a way to forgive Natasha, and maybe, just maybe, find a way to live a life that wasn't defined by the Red Room and the monsters that made her this way.

    The image of Kate's determined face flashing behind her eyelids.

    A plan, a risky one, began to take shape in her mind.

    It was a gamble, a leap of faith, but it was the only chance she had.

    Pulling her phone out of her pocket, Yelena hit send on the drafted text that had been sat open on her phone since she left Virginia.

    I’m in.

    Chapter 34

    Chapter Notes and i'm here for a second time today!

    it's christmas in june people and possibly my favourite chapter i've ever written :) The mug of tea, now lukewarm, felt heavy in Yelena's hand as she pushed herself up from the couch. The weight of her thoughts threatened to drag her down, she needed a distraction, a moment to clear her head before the chaos that was to be Christmas Eve morning. With a sigh, she decided to reunite with the dogs.

    The basement stairs creaked open with a familiar groan, and Yelena was immediately met with a furry onslaught. Lucky, the golden retriever, launched herself at Yelena's waist, tail wagging a blur, while Fanny, her own akita, lumbered over with a low whine, demanding her share of attention. Yelena chuckled, dropping down to her knees and burying her face in Fanny's soft fur as Lucky tried to lick her whole face. The comforting warmth and unconditional love radiating from the dogs were a balm to her soul, even if only for a moment.

    Across the room, a muffled voice emanated from a headset. Cooper, hunched over a beanbag chair, was clearly engrossed in some online battle. He barely registered Yelena's arrival, his thumbs flying across a controller as he issued rapid-fire commands. Until the flurry of movement from the dogs obviously caught his eye. He glanced round, expecting to see them wrestling over a chew toy, but instead, his gaze landed on Yelena.

    Her silhouette framed by the doorway, backlit by the overhead light, surprised him for a moment. "Yelena!" he exclaimed, the headset clattering to the floor with a forgotten thud, the controller still held tightly in his hands, thumbs moving over the buttons without the boys eyes even on the screen. A wide grin spread across his face, erasing any trace of his earlier focus. “When did you get here? Is Kate here? Is my Dad back?” Cooper’s question’s were rambled out much like Yelena imagined Kate’s would’ve been had it been her sat on the beanbag chair.

    A playful jab escaped the assassins lips before she could stop it. "From the way you ordered your questions, one might think Clint wasn't even here. Is your Dad chopped…? What’s the thing you say?”

    “Liver?” Cooper sheepishly rubbed the back of his neck.

    “Да. That’s the one. So глупый.” Yelena chuckled softly, as she looked away from the teenage boy in front of her and back to the two dogs still lovingly getting affection from her never stilling hands. Maybe, just maybe, a little puppy chaos was exactly what she needed, "Anyway little Barton one, we got here just a bit ago. Kate's upstairs settling in. And yeah, your Dad's back, probably snoring like a lumberjack.”

    Cooper's grin returned. "Snoring, huh? Sounds about right. So, why aren't you asleep, then?" Yelena fired the same question back at him, raising an eyebrow playfully. "Why aren't you asleep, Cooper? Shouldn't you be rather than facing whatever alien invasion you are battling on there?" The blonde nodded to the tv screen across from the boy, a title screen flashing on the screen from where Cooper had paused his game.

    Cooper's smile faltered slightly, a flicker of something unfamiliar crossing his features. "Holidays are kinda hard to sleep through," he mumbled, scuffing his slippers against the floor. "Especially the ones where Dad is supposed to be here."

    Yelena's playful expression softened. She understood better than most the weight of a parent's absence, the ache of an empty chair at the table.

    "I used to wait up for him.” Cooper said, avoiding her gaze. "Always hoped he'd make it back in time, even if it meant getting a few hours less sleep. I don’t know why I still do it, most of the time it ends in disappointment anyway." A faint, almost inaudible sigh escaped his lips. "Guess old habits die hard."

    "Believe me, Cooper," Yelena said, her voice low and sincere, "I know better than most how hard habits are to break. Especially the ones rooted in hope." She reached out a hand, gently scratching Lucky behind the ears as the dog thumped his tail against the floor. "Sometimes, even when we know it might lead to disappointment, I hold on to those slivers of hope. It's what keeps me alive, you know? Don’t have much else to live for."

    Cooper looked up at her then, a question flickering in his eyes. "Even if the hope seems… foolish?"

    Yelena smiled, a hint of sadness lingering in her gaze. "Maybe especially then," she replied. "The things that seem the most foolish are the ones worth holding onto the most." Cooper seemed to weigh her words; his teenage face etched with a seriousness Yelena recognised from Clint’s own. Finally, he spoke, his voice barely a whisper. "Are you talking about…the Red Room?"

    Yelena's breath hitched. Surprise flickered across her face, quickly masked by a steely resolve. She hadn't expected her words to touch upon the secrets she guarded so fiercely. A part of her wanted to shut down the conversation, to retreat back into the comfortable banter they had been sharing. But something in Cooper's hopeful gaze gave her pause. Yelena sighed; the sound heavy in the quiet room. It wasn't a sound of defeat, but rather a weight being lifted, a dam creaking open ever so slightly. Cooper's question had struck a chord deep within her, a melody she hadn't dared play in years.

    "The Red Room," she began, her voice rough with disuse, "it wasn't a place that fostered hope. It was a place designed to extinguish it, to mold us into something… obedient." She paused, the memory of the sterile white walls and the ever-present feeling of being watched causing a shiver to run down her spine. Yelena held her pause for a moment, carefully choosing her next words as to not traumatise another teenager on the planet. "Nights were always the hardest," she continued, her voice barely a whisper, "in the quiet darkness, even a trained killer needs a way to escape. So, I used to dream, Cooper. I dreamt of things that felt impossible – sunlight on my skin, the taste of something sweet, the freedom to choose what I wanted to do.” She looked at Cooper, her gaze filled with a vulnerability she hadn't shown to anyone years, aside from Kate.

    "Those dreams, those foolish, childish dreams, were the only comfort I had. For a few precious moments, they allowed me to forget the floor that was always cold, the needles that always pricked, the girls around me who cried themselves to sleep… for a few precious moments I could believe that Natasha and I had become grown adults together, I’d have friends, family dinners and… a dog.” Yelena fell silent, her gaze focused on Fanny down by her knee. The akita’s wide eyes watching the blonde avidly.

    Yelena couldn’t deny she felt a little lighter, a little less suffocated. Sharing a sliver of her truth with Cooper had offered a sliver of solace, a reminder that she wasn't alone in the shadows she carried. Maybe, in sharing her story, she had offered Cooper a glimpse into the resilience of the human spirit, a testament to the power of hope, even in the most desperate of circumstances. Yelena hoped the miniature Barton would carry her story and remember it, for he owed no one anything.

    A soft whine and a furry nudge at her knee pulled Yelena from her thoughts. Looking down, she met the concerned gaze of Fanny, the golden retriever, her tail thumping a steady rhythm against the carpeted floor. A small smile tugged at Yelena's lips.

    Cooper, his face etched with a mixture of empathy and awe, spoke softly. "I'm glad you and Auntie Nat are okay. That you both got out of there. I don’t know much, but I know that.” His voice, though young, held a maturity that surprised Yelena. The weight of his father's dangerous missions, the constant fear of him not coming home, it had etched its own lines on Cooper's face, lines that mirrored some of the ones Yelena saw reflected in her own reflection.

    Yelena squeezed Fanny's fur gently, finding comfort in the dog's warmth. "I hope I will be okay someday, Cooper," she replied, her voice a touch stronger. "I hope so too. And maybe, just maybe, someday those hopeful dreams won't be so foolish after all." A moment of comfortable silence settled between them, broken only by the soft snores of Lucky in the corner.

    Cooper, his gaze thoughtful, finally spoke. "Are you staying for Christmas? Are you all staying, or will you up and leave before the actual day?" he asked, his voice barely a whisper. Yelena looked at him, surprised by the question, there was obviously a deeper story there. "I… I hope so," The blonde admitted hesitantly, unsure of why she was spilling her guts to the teenage son of the man she tried to kill this time last year. "It is not easy for me to be here." She gestured vaguely around the room, indicating more to the farm generally. "Why not?" Cooper's brow furrowed in concern. "Is it because of Dad? I know you have a weird history but I thou-“ Yelena shook her head, a sad smile gracing her lips. "No, it's not him. It's…" She hesitated, unsure how to explain the turmoil within her and if she should, "It's Christmas. It's family. It's all the things I never had and all the things I lost."

    Cooper spoke, his voice surprisingly firm for his teenage years.

    "But you do have family, Yelena," he said. "You just…lost them for a while. But they were always there, waiting for you to find your way back." Cooper looked at her with a sincerity that warmed her heart. "And you have us now, too. You have Mom, Dad, Lila and me, plus Nate doesn’t stop talking about his really cool Auntie Yelena, you know." A hint of a mischievous grin flickered across his face. "Also, I'm pretty sure your sister is literally in the same house as us right now."

    The weight in her chest, once an immovable boulder, began to crumble at the edges. A lump formed in Yelena’s throat, rendering her speechless. Cooper, sensing her turmoil, offered a reassuring smile.

    "You don't have to say anything, you know," he said gently. "I get it. This whole family thing…it's gotta be weird. Trust me, with Dad and Auntie Nat back around, 'normal' is about as likely as Santa showing up in a fighter jet." The boy chuckled, the sound dispelling the tension in the air.

    The blonde settled herself against the cool concrete wall, the roughness a grounding sensation against the whirlwind of emotions churning within her. Cooper, picking up on her unspoken request to keep his company, scooted his beanbag chair a meter closer, creating a comfortable space between them.

    "So," Cooper began, his voice breaking the comfortable silence, "what did you think of that alien invasion game I was playing?" He gestured to the TV screen, a hopeful glint in his eyes. Yelena chuckled, a genuine sound this time. "Maybe," she said, her voice stronger than it had been in a long time, "we can discuss alien invasions over some hot chocolate after you tell me all about what you, Lila and Nate have been up to."

    A grin, wide and genuine, erupted on Cooper's face. As he launched into a detailed explanation of his mischievous younger sister and her array of boyfriends, Yelena found herself leaning in, a flicker of warmth blooming in her chest.

    Laura peeked into the dimly lit basement, a smile widening at the sight. There, sprawled out on the worn leather sofa, was Yelena, fast asleep. A fleece blanket, clearly not meant for her petite frame, lay haphazardly across her form. Fanny was curled up contentedly at her feet, a rhythmic rise and fall of her chest the only sign of movement.

    Laura's gaze shifted to the other side of the room, where a sight even more unexpected met her eyes. Cooper was nestled in the beanbag chair, his long limbs contorted at impossible angles. Lucky was draped across his lap, in a position Laura couldn’t understand to be comfortable, his snores a low rumble that vibrated through the room. A stray controller lay forgotten on the floor, testament to her son’s late-night gaming session. Laura couldn't help but let out a soft chuckle. For a moment, she simply stood there, watching the peaceful tableau before her. The weight of the past year, the constant fear and uncertainty, seemed to melt away in the face of this simple scene.

    The rhythmic sizzle of pancakes filled the kitchen as Laura tiptoed back upstairs. Clint, clad in a festive (though slightly ketchup-stained) Christmas sweater, was hunched over a massive bowl, expertly cracking two dozen eggs with one hand. Laura couldn't help but smile. Clint's chaotic energy might drive her crazy at times, but there was a comforting familiarity to these Christmas mornings, a tradition that transcended even the threats that came their way so often.

    Reaching the kitchen, Laura slid into the space beside Clint, the warmth of the stove radiating around them. "They're still sleeping," she murmured, leaning into his side. Clint glanced up, a mischievous glint in his eyes. "Who? The aliens? Cause I swear that game is never turned off."

    Laura rolled her eyes, swatting his arm playfully. "No, silly. Cooper and Yelena. They must have talked all night."

    Clint's grin widened. "Huh, unexpected! Let them sleep. We need all the energy we can get for whatever craziness we're about to face when Nate gets down here." He expertly flipped the scrambled eggs, his movements practiced from years of Christmas morning breakfasts. Laura chuckled, flipping the pancakes on the griddle. "You sound awfully optimistic considering we have a two Black Widow assassins in a fight, your protégé who is practically facing her death and three very chaotic children under one roof. And oh, let’s not forget the two dogs, neither of which listen to anyone’s instruction."

    Clint chuckled, expertly plating the fluffy eggs. "Ah, but that's the beauty of family, Laura. It wouldn't be complete without a little chaos." He gestured to the bowls of batter and mountains of ingredients laid out on the counter. "The more the merrier, right? Even if the 'merry' involves flour fights and Lucky chasing squirrels through the living room." Laura considered this, turning the last pancake with a practiced flick of her wrist. It was true. Despite the looming threats from, well, it seemed everyone, there was a sense of…something different this Christmas.

    "Well lets maybe miss out the squirrel part… you know," Laura said, flipping the last pancake, and adding almost as If it was a sudden realisation, "for a man who cracks eggs like a pro-chef, you make a terrible mess." Laura took the plate from him, a smile lighting up her face.

    Clint grinned, wiping a stray bit of egg yolk from his beard.

    A loud thump echoed from the stairs, followed by a chorus of giggles. Laura and Clint exchanged a look, both a mixture of exasperation and amusement in their eyes. Speaking of chaos, here it came.

    At the top of the stairs stood Natasha, her hair a mess of sleep braids, clad in a pair of flannel pyjamas that looked far too big for her. In her arms, Nate clung sleepily, his brown hair sticking out at odd angles. Beside them, Lila bounced on the balls of her feet, her eyes bright with excitement bursting to be let out in some form.

    "Hold on there, tiger! First things first. Breakfast is calling, and then we can discuss whatever it is bursting at your seams.” Clint said to Lila as he walked up beside her, placing a kiss on the top of her head before reaching out and ruffling Nate’s hair, making it even more of a mess than it was already.

    He shot a glance at Natasha, a silent plea for help.

    Natasha, despite the weariness in her eyes, couldn't help but laugh at the sight. This chaotic, messy family of theirs, it was a far cry from the solitary life she had known. But as she met Clint's gaze, a silent understanding passed between them. For all the danger and darkness, they faced, this, this breakfast table filled with their children's chatter, was something worth fighting for.

    "Alright, troops," Natasha said, her voice surprisingly firm for someone who looked like she hadn't slept a wink. "Your dad’s right. Breakfast first, and Lila, honey," she added, gently nudging the over-excited girl towards a chair, "tell me all about Nate's chatter over pancakes."

    Lila, momentarily distracted by the promise of breakfast, scurried towards the table, a whirlwind of colourful pyjamas and boundless energy. Nate, finally roused from his sleep- induced haze, looked around with bleary eyes before burying his face back in Natasha's neck. The redhead settled Nate into his chair, gently tugging his arms off from around her neck, before taking a seat next to him, the boy leaning back into her side, seemingly content with the comprise.

    Laura, catching the scene from the doorway, couldn't help but smile. There was something undeniably sweet about seeing Natasha, the world's deadliest assassin, reduced to an attentive auntie by a sleepy toddler.

    "You three tuck in," Laura said, gesturing towards the spread building in front of them. "I'll go wake Cooper. Clint, you get to play negotiator with Lila over how crispy the bacon gets." The woman said with a smirk as she patted her husband’s back on her way past. Reaching the basement stairs, she started heading down and before Laura even got halfway, a mumbled voice startled her.

    "Morning," came a groggy groan from the bottom step. Cooper, his hair sticking up at odd angles and looking the twin of his little brother, his eyes barely open, shuffled into view as he climbed up towards his mom. He was clearly still clinging to the remnants of sleep, but the undeniable aroma of breakfast wafting from downstairs had managed to pull him from his slumber.

    "Rough night, Coop?" Laura asked, a smile tugging at her lips.

    Cooper managed a weak grin in return. "Rough morning, more like it. Note to self, don’t sleep on a beanbag." He rubbed his eyes with the heel of his hand, blinking away the last vestiges of sleep.

    "Is Yelena awake?"

    Cooper glanced back towards the basement, his voice lowering slightly. "I... I'm not sure. She was still looking like she was asleep when I woke up, and I didn't want to startle her if she wasn't."

    Laura nodded in understanding. They both knew Natasha was a creature of habit, and waking her without warning could be... unpredictable. It was smart for Coop to assume the same. "Okay," Laura whispered back, "well, breakfast is calling. Why don't we head upstairs and join the others? I’ll go see if Kate is up instead.”

    Cooper shuffled into the kitchen resembling a particularly disgruntled dandelion, Laura following after him with a chuckle. Clint, spatula in hand, burst out laughing. "Well, look who decided to join the party! Morning, Coop! Sleep well? You look like your brother.” Cooper swatted playfully at Clint's arm, a sheepish grin spreading across his face. "Hilarious, Dad.” The boy said as Clint brought him into his side with one arm.

    Catching Clint’s eye, Laura smiled softly at the pair. "Looks like Yelena's still enjoying her sleep." The woman of the house said to her husband, receiving a nod in return. With that, she patted his shoulder and headed for the stairs.

    Reaching the first floor, Laura paused in front of Kate's bedroom door. Taking a deep breath, she knocked softly. A muffled "Come in" drifted through the door. Pushing it open a crack, Laura peeked inside.

    Kate was sprawled across her bed, fully clothed but still nestled under the covers. Her brow was furrowed in concentration as she scrolled through something on her phone. "Morning, Kate," Laura said gently, pushing the door open a little further. Kate looked up, "Oh, hey Laura," she mumbled, her voice thick with sleep. Laura noticed the tension radiating from Kate and gestured towards the phone in her hand. "What's got you looking like you just wrestled a rogue reindeer?"

    Kate sighed, her shoulders slumping. "Look at this." She sat up against the headboard behind her and held up her phone, turning the screen towards Laura. An article headline blazed across the top of the New York Times webpage.
