    ‘Checkmate: The Last Bishop Graces New York’s Elite Circles at Annual Christmas Party’ For years, the Bishop Christmas Party has been a prominent fixture on the New York social calendar. Hosted by the enigmatic Eleanor Bishop, a titan of the tech industry and notorious businesswoman, the event was a byword for extravagance and exclusivity. Following Mrs Bishop’s passing a couple of months ago, the future of the party remained shrouded in mystery up until a couple of weeks before when word leaked to the press that the event would go ahead.

    And last night, amidst the swirling snowflakes and twinkling lights of a Manhattan winter, the Bishop name returned to the spotlight.

    Gone are the days of Eleanor Bishop's stark minimalism. Jack Duquesne, her fiancé and the organizer of this year's event, opted for a decidedly more opulent approach. The ballroom, once a canvas of cool whites and brushed steel, was now transformed into a flashy winter wonderland. Crystal snowflakes cascaded from the ceiling, glittering like fallen stars. Lush evergreens adorned the walls, and a towering Christmas tree, adorned with priceless ornaments and strings of sparkling fairy lights, held court in the centre of the room, draped in golds to match the rest of the room’s décor.

    Despite initial scepticism from some quarters, Duquesne proved himself a capable host, infusing the event with his own unique flair while paying homage to Eleanor's legendary sense of style. Guests seemed to marvel at the elegant decor and impeccable attention to detail, with many noting Jack's seamless transition into his role as the acting head of the Bishop household.

    Among the A-listers and social climbers vying for lucrative business deals with their fellow socialites, another familiar face walked the crowds.

    Kate Bishop made a striking appearance at the annual Christmas party hosted in the name of her illustrious family. The event, renowned for its opulence and grandeur, saw a fresh breath of life as Kate, the heiress to the Bishop fortune, stepped back into the spotlight after a period of absence following her mother's tragic passing.

    The night was filled with whispered conversations, speculative glances, and the clinking of champagne flutes. Musicians, shrouded in shimmering silver attire, played a hauntingly beautiful melody, adding to the air of intrigue that seemed to follow the last surviving, Bishop. One by one, celebrities, socialites, and even a few rumoured foreign dignitaries found themselves drawn to Miss Bishop’s enigmatic presence.

    Notably, Miss Bishop was not alone in her return to the social scene. Throughout the evening, she was accompanied by a striking blonde, not known to sources close to the family. The pair seemed inseparable, sharing whispered conversations, and exchanging knowing glances as they navigated the crowded ballroom. Observers noted that Miss Bishop and her companion spent a great deal of time at the bar, where they engaged in lively conversation with two of Kate's college friends, adding a touch of familiarity to the otherwise glamorous affair. A notable absence, however, was that of Clint Barton (Hawkeye), who had been spotted at last year's event. This raised eyebrows among annual attendees, as it was not widely known that the Bishops had any connection to the enigmatic figure. His absence from this years event has sparked speculation about the true nature of his relationship with the family and absence in recent years from the public eye.

    As the night drew to a close, and the last strains of music faded into the ether, the question on everyone's lips remained: What comes next for Miss Kate Bishop? Her return to the spotlight, has left the elite circles of New York society buzzing with speculation and bursting with questions.

    Will she continue to grace the city's most exclusive events, filling her mother’s place among the social elite? Or will she retreat once again into the shadows, leaving behind only whispers and rumours of her existence?

    Indeed, as the city's elite speculate on Miss Bishop's next move, another drama looms on the horizon: the upcoming mayoral race. With Kingpin's shadow looming large over the political landscape, and rumours swirling of clandestine alliances and backroom deals, New York City braces itself for a battle of epic proportions.

    In this high-stakes game of power and influence, one can't help but wonder if Miss Bishop will emerge as a player or a pawn. Will she navigate the treacherous waters of New York's political arena with the same skill and finesse she displays in the world of high society? Only time will tell.

    As the city holds its breath in anticipation of what lies ahead, one thing remains certain: with a Bishop back in the spotlight, the stage is set for a spectacle unlike any other. And as the city prepares for the drama to unfold, all eyes will be on the Last Bishop, watching to see what role she will play in shaping the future of New York City.

    -

    A defeated sigh escaped Laura's lips as she shut Kate's bedroom door behind her. Heading downstairs, she found the remnants of chaotic breakfast barely clinging to life. Nate was a whirlwind of sugar-fuelled energy, chattering excitedly about Santa with a begrudging teenage Cooper, who was valiantly attempting to shovel pancakes into his mouth while simultaneously fending off playful attacks from a giggling Lila, intent on annoying her older brother as much as possible.

    Natasha, looking surprisingly content with the noise for someone who had probably slept less than a squirrel on espresso, was trying to convince Nate that another spoonful of maple syrup wasn't a good idea.

    "Looks like the party's already started," Laura called out, a wry smile playing on her lips. Natasha glanced up, a flicker of amusement crossing her features. "Don't worry, we've managed to contain the chaos – for now."

    Laura pulled out a chair and slid into it, her gaze scanning the room. “Lila, stop waving the knife in the air.”

    "But Dad went to check on the waffles ages ago! I’m knifing the air in protest." Lila declared, pointing a sticky finger towards the direction of the kitchen counter.

    Following Lila's finger, Laura saw Clint, spatula in hand, attempting to wrestle a particularly stubborn waffle iron into submission. His brow was furrowed in concentration, and a light dusting of flour decorated his apron like a badge of honour.

    "Looks like he's facing a formidable foe," Laura said, trying to stifle a laugh. Kate slowly stalked down the stairs whilst Laura snorted at Clint’s latest attempt to coax the stubborn waffle from the iron. The brunette had brushed and thrown her hair back in a ponytail. The archer appeared beside Laura and held her phone out, screen pointed towards Clint. "I need to show him this, Laura," she said in a whisper.

    Laura nodded, understanding dawning in her eyes. There was no time for a private conversation, not with the kids practically bouncing off the walls. With a sigh, she turned to Kate and gave her a squeeze on the shoulder.

    Kate didn't need any further encouragement. She simply stretched her arm out over Laura's head, the phone hovering precariously in the air for a moment before landing squarely in Clint's flour-dusted hand. He looked up, a confused expression on his face, before his gaze met Laura's. A silent exchange passed between them, a question in his eyes, a warning in hers.

    The empty breakfast plates were stacked precariously in the sink, the remnants of a chaotic but satisfying meal. Laura wiped down the counter, a tired but satisfied smile playing on her lips. The leftovers had been wrapped and placed in the fridge, free for nibbling throughout the day as no more cooking would be done until Christmas Dinner the next day. Outside, the muffled sounds of laughter and excited shrieks filtered through the window. Cooper, ever the reluctant babysitter, could be heard trying to convince a particularly exuberant Lila that tackling him into a snowdrift was not a good idea. Fanny and Lucky were surprisingly thick as thieves, cavorting in the snow with all the enthusiasm of puppies. Clint, leaning against the doorway with a mug of coffee cradled in his hands, watched the scene unfold with a hint of a wistful smile on his face. "Looks like they're having fun," he said, his voice rough with unspoken emotions.

    Laura turned, a silent agreement passing between them. It wasn't perfect, this makeshift family they'd built, but in this moment, with the snow falling gently outside and the sounds of laughter filling the air, there was a sense of…something real. Something genuine. Something they were fiercely determined to protect.

    "Speaking of fun," Laura said, her voice teasing, "what’d you think of that article Kate showed you?”

    Clint winced. The phone Laura had retrieved from Kate was now clutched tightly in his hand, the article about the Bishop Christmas Party glaring back at him.

    Just then, Cooper burst through the kitchen door, a dusting of snow clinging to his hair and cheeks. Lucky, dripping snowmelt and sporting a triumphant doggy grin, trotted in behind him.

    "Hey, can you one of you guys help me with Lila?" Cooper pleaded. "She's convinced she can build a snowman taller than the house."

    Laura and Clint exchanged a glance, a wry smile on each of their faces. "Natasha!" Clint bellowed, his voice carrying through the house. A few moments later, Natasha appeared at the top of the stairs, a questioning look on her face. Cooper took the initiative handed to him on a silver platter. He scurried over to Natasha, grabbing a forgotten coat hanging on a nearby hook and shoving it into her arms. "You’re my backup!” he declared with a mischievous grin, already pulling her towards the back door. Natasha chuckled, her playful side peeking through. "Alright, alright," she conceded, allowing Cooper to drag her outside. "An explanation would be nice!” Her voice trailed off as the door slammed behind the two racing out onto the lawn.

    "It's not good.” Clint spoke as the voices outside grew smaller, Laura’s gaze turning from the window to her husbands side profile, “Especially not for Kate. With everything going on, having this many eyes on her…." He trailed off, his brow furrowed in concern. Clint continued, "Kate gets restless being cooped up all the time and shutting her down completely isn't the answer. She's a fighter, Laura. If we keep her muzzled, she'll find another way to blow off steam, and that’s not going to be pretty.”

    Laura sighed, the warmth of the kitchen suddenly feeling stifling. "So, what do we do?" Laura asked, her frustration simmering.

    "We'll trust her judgement.”

    Laura gawked at him as if he had lost his mind. "Clint," she began, her voice barely a whisper, "are you serious? We can't just—"

    Yelena emerged from the basement, her expression unreadable, but the couple knew she had most likely heard the whole conversation. The blonde glanced between Clint and Laura. "Barton…" she began, her voice measured. “is right.” Yelena’s face may have actually paled as those words exited her mouth and as Clint smirked, "But… up to a point.” The assassin held up a finger to signify to Clint she wasn’t done. “We can't just sit back and let her roam free. She will die.”

    Clint nodded in agreement, his gaze meeting Yelena's with a silent understanding. Laura sighed, running a hand through her hair as she considered their words. "Fine," she relented, her voice resigned. "But if anything… and I mean anything, happens to that sweet girl… you’ll both be answering to me.” It wasn't an empty threat. Laura, despite her calm demeanour, was a fierce protector of her family, and Kate had become an important part of that family.

    With a decision made, Clint turned to Yelena, curiosity flickering in his eyes. "Speaking of Kate," he began, "did Sonya fill you in on what happened while you were… indisposed?" Yelena shook her head, a frown creasing her brow. "No.”

    Clint launched into a quick explanation, catching Yelena up on the events she'd missed. He filled her in about Kate's concern for her well-being, the whole hawk drone situation, and Sonya's surprise visit – which, based on Yelena's barely suppressed smirk, Clint took as confirmation she was the very reason Sonya had shown up in the first place. Clint's smile faltered. "And then," he continued, his voice turning serious, "Kate kind of blew up at everyone. She started shouting about how if we kept keeping secrets from her, then she may well not even be here and wished for Kingpin and Valentina to be the ones to do it." Yelena's grin vanished, replaced by a look of concern. "She… she said that?" she asked, her voice barely above a whisper.

    “Judging by the state of her knuckles, I'd say the punching bag in the gym took the brunt of it afterwards." Laura added in, having wanted to ask Kate what was under her bandages when she arrived last night, but didn’t get a chance.

    Yelena winced, a wave of shame washing over her. She hadn't even noticed Kate's injuries. Here she was, focused on her own recovery and the tangle of emotions it brought up, completely ignoring her friend and her pain.

    Yelena mumbled, her voice barely audible. "I hadn't noticed."

    Laura offered a sympathetic nod. "You've had other things on your mind, Yelena. Don't beat yourself up about it. Kate’s been hurt worse. She’s okay."

    Yelena shook her head, her denial laced with a tremor of guilt. "No, it's not that. I should’ve noticed. I don’t miss a thing, Laura Barton.” Her voice hardened, a flicker of her past training momentarily breaking through the tentative camaraderie. The blonde glanced towards the doorway, a hint of determination hardening her gaze. "I'll find her." With that, she turned and walked out of the kitchen, her steps purposeful.

    The afternoon melted into early evening, the once playful shouts from outside replaced by a tense silence that hung heavy in the air. Kate was missing. Not vanished-without-a-trace missing, but simply…gone. No one had seen her since the breakfast and the collective parental anxiety in the Barton household had reached a fever pitch.

    Clint and Laura, along with Natasha and Cooper, had retraced their steps a dozen times, searching every nook and cranny of the farmhouse. Even Lila contributed to the frantic search with tearful pleas for Kate to stop messing around. Yelena, uncharacteristically on edge, had scoured the immediate vicinity, a growing sense of unease gnawing at her. Kate could be a handful, but this…this silence was unsettling.

    As the last rays of sunlight dipped below the horizon, casting long, skeletal shadows across the snowy fields, Laura, her voice strained with worry, called for a halt to the search. "We need a plan," she declared, her gaze meeting Clint's.

    A wet nose nudged Yelena's hand. Looking down, she saw Lucky, Kate's perpetually crazy hound, gazing up at her with soulful brown eyes. A spark of inspiration ignited in Yelena's mind. Dogs, she knew, were often remarkably good at tracking their humans. Glancing over at Clint, she suggested, "Лаки, иди сюда.” The retriever sensing the urgency in her voice, thumped his nose against her leg.

    Clint, understanding dawning on his face, "You think…"

    Yelena nodded, a hint of a plan forming. "It's worth a shot. And maybe," she added, eyeing her own akita sprawled contentedly by the fireplace, "we could use some additional muscle." The blonde let out a low whistle. Fanny, ever obedient, slowly rose to her feet, tail wagging furiously as she reached Yelena.

    With a renewed sense of purpose, Yelena and the canines headed out into the gathering dusk. The air was crisp and cold, the snow crunching softly under their boots. Lucky, his nose glued to the ground, led the way, his short legs pumping determinedly. Fanny, trotting close behind, seemed to be picking up on Lucky's scent, her powerful legs carrying her effortlessly through the deepening snow. The rest of the earlier grouped search party had stayed in the warm, needing Nate and Lila to calm down before bedtime.

    Yelena followed the trail deeper into the woods behind the farmhouse, the towering pines forming a dark, silent cathedral around them. The search became more difficult as the darkness intensified, but neither dogs faltered, keeping Yelena following them further and further from the house. Finally, after what felt like an eternity, Lucky let out a low whine and veered off the path, his tail wagging furiously.

    Yelena and Fanny followed, pushing through a thicket of snow-laden branches until they emerged into a small clearing. There, nestled at the midpoint of a large pine tree, stood a rickety old treehouse. A lone figure sat huddled beneath it, sat on the floor, back against the trunk, was a mop of brown hair visible in the faint moonlight.

    "Kate?" Yelena called out softly.

    The figure beneath the treehouse stirred. "Yelena?" came a muffled reply. Relief washed over Yelena as Kate was made visible from her hiding spot as she got closer. The archer had a dusting of snow clinging to her hair and clothes. Her eyes were red-rimmed and puffy.

    "What are you doing маленький ястреб?" Yelena asked, concern softening her voice. Kate shrugged, scuffing her boots in the snow, as she kicked out her legs, not making any effort to stand. "I just needed some… space," she mumbled.

    Yelena crouched down beside Kate, the snow crunching under her knees. The girl looked small and vulnerable huddled beneath the treehouse, a stark contrast to the fierce spirit Yelena normally witnessed. Yelena shrugged off her own coat, a thick woollen garment that would hopefully offer some warmth. Ignoring Kate's mumbled protests, Yelena gently draped the coat over Kate's shoulders. The material was heavy and warm, instantly enveloping Kate in a cocoon of heat.

    Kate flinched slightly, she peeked up at Yelena through her eyelashes, a hint of confusion warring with the gratitude in her eyes. "You… confuse me." she mumbled; her voice barely audible.

    Yelena met her gaze, a hint of a smile playing on her lips. "Maybe," she admitted, "but it's freezing out here. And I am not going to let you freeze, no matter how confusing I am.” Kate stared at her for a long moment, obviously still confused.

    "Can I… can I stay here for a while?" Kate asked finally, her voice barely a whisper. "Just for a little bit longer?"

    Yelena looked around at the small clearing, the snow-covered branches forming a protective canopy overhead. There was a sense of peace here, a quiet solitude that seemed to resonate with Kate's mood.

    “Да,” Yelena said gently, “we can stay here a while.” She settled down next to Kate, leaning back against the rough bark of the tree. The silence returned. As they sat there, side by side beneath the old treehouse, Yelena couldn't help but steal glances at Kate. The young woman seemed lost in thought, her gaze fixed on a distant point in the star-dusted sky. Yelena wondered what secrets those eyes held, what questions were undoubtedly brimming under their stormy surface.

    They sat there for a long while. Lucky, ever the anomaly, seemed unfazed by the late hour. His short legs pumped furiously as he chased rogue snowflakes, his excited barks echoing through the silent woods. Fanny, on the other hand, seemed to understand the mood. With a soft whimper, she settled down beside Kate, her head resting gently on the young archer's thigh. The warmth of the dog's fur and the steady rhythm of her breathing provided a surprising comfort to Kate, a silent reassurance in the face of her swirling emotions. Yelena stole another glance at Kate. The girl's face, illuminated by the soft glow of the moon reflecting off the snow, was a mask of emotions. Hurt flickered in her eyes, but there was also a flicker of anxiety, a part of the Hawkeye woman that Yelena didn’t like to experience. Yelena finally broke the silence, her voice barely a whisper, "Clint told me what you said… back at the Compound.”

    Kate's head snapped up, her gaze meeting Yelena's with a mixture of surprise and apprehension. "What did I say?" she mumbled, her voice thick with emotion. Yelena hesitated for a moment, unsure how to proceed. Did she push for honesty, or offer a silent understanding? In the end, she opted for a compromise.

    "You said you felt alone," Yelena said gently. "Like no one was telling you anything." Kate looked away, toeing her boot at a clump of snow. "Oh. That.” she mumbled. "It's just... I want to help. But everyone keeps treating me like a kid who needs to be protected from the big bad world."

    Yelena understood the feeling all too well. She'd spent years feeling like a pawn in someone else's game, kept in the dark and used as a weapon. She sighed; a sound laced with a lifetime of weariness. "You're not some outsider, Kate." Yelena said firmly, her voice laced with conviction. "This isn't about keeping you out. Believe me, if I could tell you everything, I would."

    “So why keep me in the dark? Keep all these secrets? Why do you constantly shut me out?” Kate’s voice grew louder, the hurt and anger bubbling over.

    Yelena held up a hand, silencing Kate with a gesture that spoke of years of training. "Are we still talking about the same thing, Kate?" she asked, a hint of exasperation creeping into her voice. "Because the reason you're not getting the full picture has nothing to do with a lack of trust in you, and instead everything to do with protecting you from a world you barely understand."

    Kate scoffed. "Protecting me? From what? The people trying to kill me? Or are you protecting me from you? Answer that question and I'll tell you if we're talking about the same thing or not."

    Yelena's eyes narrowed. Kate's words hit a nerve, a raw truth that hung heavy in the air. Protecting Kate from the likes of Valentina or Kingpin, that was one thing. But what Kate was insinuating… was a whole different ballgame.

    Yelena shook her head, a frustrated sigh escaping her lips. “К черту это,” she muttered under her breath, “I am not having this conversation with you right now, Kate.” “Right now or ever? You never want to talk Yelena.” Kate shot back, “You’re like… drawing blood from a stone! Impossible!” Her frustration peaked, her shout stopping Lucky in his tracks mid-snow chase. He looked back at them with confused brown eyes, his tail wagging hesitantly.

    "Protecting? You think I need protecting?" Kate continued, her voice trembling slightly. "From what? What are you all so afraid of? This is my fight too, you know! More mine than any of yours! And you all get to run in blindly without a second thought!” Yelena winced at the raw truth in Kate's words. They were a stark reminder of their own failures, of how their need for control had inadvertently pushed Kate further away. "It's not about that," Yelena started, her voice softer this time.

    "Then what is it about?" Kate interrupted, her frustration barely contained. "Because from where I'm standing, it looks a whole lot like you don't trust me. You don't trust me to handle the truth, you don't trust me to fight my own battles. Well, guess what? I don't need your protection, Yelena. And if you're not going to be honest with me, if you're not going to be part of the solution, then maybe you should just leave."

    The harsh words hung heavy in the air, the weight of them settling on Yelena's shoulders like a physical blow. She stared at Kate, a mix of emotions swirling in her eyes: hurt, anger, but most of all, a grudging respect for the young woman's strength.

    "You need to come inside," Yelena finally managed, her voice firm but laced with a hint of helplessness. "You're freezing."

    Kate's anger flared anew. "You just did it again. You dismiss me just like that!" she shouted, her voice echoing through the silent woods. "I just poured out my heart and all you can say is I'm cold?"

    Yelena winced. This wasn't just about the secrets anymore. Kate was feeling completely dismissed, like a child with no agency. It mirrored a feeling Yelena knew all too well, a feeling that had festered within her for years – the feeling of being unseen, unheard, by Eleanor. She understood that now, with a painful clarity that made her stomach churn. "No, Kate," Yelena said, trying to bridge the widening chasm between them. "That's not what I meant. I… I just..." She stumbled for the right words, frustration gnawing at her. "You just what?" Kate challenged, her voice trembling, "You just want to shove me back inside my box, pretend everything's okay, and keep me in the dark? Well, guess what, Yelena? It's not okay anymore!"

    Yelena’s eyes glazed over for a moment, a flashback playing behind them. Natasha, vibrant and alive, pulling her into a fierce hug. The weight of a decision, heavy and final, settling fresh on Yelena's shoulders.

    "I chose Natasha," Yelena finally whispered, the words catching in her throat. "And she chose the world. That's the downfall that comes with loving a hero, Kate. They… they sacrifice everything, and sometimes, that includes themselves too."

    She looked back at Kate, her voice thick with a raw emotion she rarely allowed herself to show. "I won't let history repeat itself, Kate. “I won't let you to go down the same path I did, Kate. I won’t let you be used, manipulated, and left with nothing but scars.” Yelena's voice caught Kate off guard. For a moment, the anger drained from her, until a new question bubbled up. A humourless scoff escaped Kate's lips. "So, you think you're the only one who can handle it? The only one strong enough to handle the fight, the sleepless nights and the loss? I can assure you they are very human emotions Yelena. You’re not special.” Yelena rolled her eyes. “Боже мой. I won't be the one to teach you how to get yourself killed Kate!"

    Kate stared at her, a multitude of emotions flitting across her face. There was anger, yes, but also a grudging acknowledgement, for all her flaws, Yelena truly cared about little old her. “You're strong, Kate. Stronger than anyone gives you credit for. Stronger than you give yourself credit for.” A ghost of a smile flickered across the assassin’s lips. "But strength comes in different forms, Kate. Sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is walk away." "Should I walk away from you then?" Kate asked, her voice barely a whisper. The question hung heavy in the air, a silent plea for honesty, for connection.

    The question hung heavy in the air, a silent plea that struck Yelena with a force she hadn't anticipated. "Should I walk away from you then?" echoed in her mind, shattering the carefully constructed facade she'd presented. For a moment, she was speechless, the vulnerability in Kate's voice a stark contrast to the fierceness she'd displayed just moments ago.

    Before Yelena could formulate a response, Kate continued, her voice trembling slightly but filled with a steely resolve. "You've told me on countless occasions how dangerous you are, how bad you are. You want me away from danger… so? Should I walk away from you? From Clint? From Natasha?"

    Yelena winced. Kate's words were a stark reminder of her own brusqueness, of how her desire to protect had morphed into a wall pushing Kate further away. "No, Kate," she finally managed, her voice softer now. "That's not what I meant. That’s not what I want." "Then what did you mean?" Kate challenged; her gaze unwavering. "Because right now, it feels an awful lot like that. What do you want Yelena?” The brunette exhaled heavily, her last question coming out in a tumbling breath, as she titled her head back against the freezing tree trunk behind them.

    Yelena hesitated. It mirrored a question Yelena herself had grappled with for years. What did she truly want? The answer, she realized with a pang of longing, was something she'd buried deep within herself, a dream stolen by the Red Room.

The image faded as quickly as it appeared, leaving behind a bittersweet ache in Yelena's chest.

    "I…" Yelena began, her voice barely a whisper. "Remember what I told you about the Red Room? How they took everything from us?"

    Kate nodded.

    "They took our dreams, Kate," Yelena continued, her voice thick with emotion. "They turned us into weapons, into tools for violence. But sometimes, at night… sometimes I used to dream."

    She looked away, her gaze drifting towards the distant farmhouse. "I dreamt of a life… a normal life. A life with a family, with мама and папа, constant laughter, maybe even a dog that sheds like crazy." A ghost of a smile flickered across her lips.

    "I dreamt of a life where I didn’t have to fight anymore," Yelena whispered, the raw honesty in her voice surprising even herself. "A life where I could choose my own path.” Kate stared at her, the anger and defiance replaced by silence. She saw, not for the first time, the cracks in Yelena's carefully constructed facade, but this time it was so intense, Kate felt like she might have actually broken the blonde with her stubbornness. These weren't just cracks etched by experience, but scars left by a life stolen. Yelena had stripped herself bare to articulate herself to Kate.

    The silence stretched heavy with unspoken emotions. Kate's initial urge to fill it with questions, with reassurances, faded. She understood, with a clarity that surprised her, that Yelena wasn't finished. This wasn't a confession easily spoken, and Kate knew rushing the blonde wouldn't help.

    Yelena remained quiet for a while; her gaze fixed on a distant point on the horizon. The moonlight glinted off a lone tear that traced a path down her cheek, a crying Yelena wasn’t something Kate had experienced thus far, and the brunette froze.

    "And…” Yelena spoke, her voice barely a murmur, after what felt like an eternity. She trailed off, the single word hanging in the air like a question unanswered. But Kate knew better. This wasn't a question for her, but a hesitant step forward, a bridge tentatively extended. Kate met Yelena's gaze, a silent promise passing between them. She wouldn't push. Yelena took a deep breath, the cold air stinging her lungs. Deciding to take the plunge, she spoke, her voice barely above a whisper. "I think I dreamt of you once." Kate's eyebrows shot up in surprise. This was unexpected, a twist in their conversation that left her speechless for a moment. "You dreamt of me?" she finally managed, her voice barely a squeak.

    Yelena nodded, a small smile on her lips, her hand reaching up to absently brush a stray strand of hair from her face. "I didn't see faces," Yelena continued, her voice dropping even lower, "I dreamt of a best friend, Kate," The assassin admitted, the vulnerability in her voice raw and unexpected. "Someone who wouldn't judge me for the things I've done, or the things I've become. Someone who would see me, the real me, and love me anyway." A flicker of sadness crossed her eyes, a glimpse of the loneliness that had haunted her for years. Kate's breath hitched in her throat. Never, in all their bickering and arguments, had she expected this level of honesty from Yelena. This wasn't just about a dream; it was a confession.

    "Yelena…" Kate began, her voice thick with emotion. But the words died in her throat. What could she possibly say that would be a worthy enough answer to that?

    Before Kate could elaborate, Yelena surprised her. The blonde replaced by a sudden urgency, spun Kate around, gripping her forearms with a strength that belied her frame. "You can't walk away," Yelena said, her voice tight with a mixture of desperation and something that sounded suspiciously like fear. "You can't walk away..." Finally, the words tumbled out, raw and unfiltered.

    A sliver of golden light peeked through the blinds, painting shimmering stripes across the faces of the slumbering occupants of the Barton farmhouse. It was Christmas morning, and a sense of barely contained excitement crackled in the air.

"Let's go see if Santa paid us a visit."

    With Nate cradled against his chest, Clint padded across the room and gently knocked on Lila's bedroom door. "Lila, sweetheart, are you awake?" he called out, his voice warm with affection. Before he could even react, Lila darted past him, her small feet pattering eagerly down the stairs. Clint followed after her, his own anticipation building with each step. There was something truly magical about Christmas morning with his children, and he wouldn't miss a single moment of it.

    As the first rays of dawn fully illuminated the living room, a collective gasp erupted from the two children as they reached the bottom of the stairs. The floor in front of them was a wonderland of colourful wrapping paper, toys spilling out from beneath a magnificently decorated Christmas tree.

    Laura, ever the picture of Christmas cheer, emerged from the kitchen, a tray laden with steaming mugs of hot cocoa and a plate piled high with cinnamon rolls balanced in her hands. "Merry Christmas, sleepyheads!" she boomed, her voice filled with warmth. The children erupted into a frenzy, Nate scrambling out of Clint’s arms and diving headfirst into the mountain of presents. Lila squealed with delight as she unwrapped a new dollhouse, complete with miniature furniture. Cooper, probably woken by the screeching emerged from the basement and joined in the fun, and he was soon meticulously examining a new gaming controller.

    Clint watched the chaos with a contented smile. This, right here, was what Christmas was all about. The joy on the children's faces, the warmth of family, the feeling of togetherness that wrapped around them like a well-worn blanket.

    Natasha stood by the tree, a watchful eye on the proceedings. She had been up with Laura early this morning, helping to start Christmas on as smooth of a note as possible. Both women knew it wouldn’t last all day, but they could try their best. A comfortable silence settled between the adults, they had faced down alien armies and world-ending threats, but this, this simple domesticity, held its own kind of magic.

    The dogs added to the merriment, their tails wagging furiously as they weaved between the children, occasionally snatching a stray bow or two in their playful jaws. Their owners emerged from the staircase not long after the kids, their steps synchronized in a sleepy rhythm. Kate rubbed her eyes, still half-asleep, while Yelena stifled a yawn behind her hand. "Morning, you two.” Laura greeted them with a warm smile, cupping her mug in between both hands as she leant on the back of the couch, her eyes flicking from the two woman back to her three kids.

    "Morning," Kate mumbled, her voice groggy as she shuffled toward the enticing aroma of coffee and cinnamon rolls. Yelena only nodded in response; her movements languid as she followed Kate's lead. Yelena, perched on the edge of the couch, mesmerized by the whirlwind of activity. The sight of children, so carefree and full of life, was a stark contrast to what she had experienced and observed her whole life. The blonde watched as Kate, sat next to her, laughed as she helped Lila assemble her dollhouse from afar, a smile sneaking its way onto her sleepy face.

The air crackled with a tension that was both unfamiliar and strangely exhilarating. Then, a small smile, genuine and unguarded, touched Yelena's lips. It was a smile that seemed to light up her entire face, chasing away the shadows that usually lurked in her eyes. "Maybe…" she admitted, her voice soft as she pulled back a little.

    “Maybe…?” Kate hung on the end of the sentence.

    “Maybe,” Yelena rolled her eyes fondly, “I’m focusing on my blessings today.” The blonde whispered to Kate with an all too soppy look on her face, “Christmas seems a good of a day as any.”

"I didn't see faces," Yelena continued, her voice dropping even lower, "I dreamt of a best friend, Kate," The assassin admitted, the vulnerability in her voice raw and unexpected. "Someone who wouldn't judge me for the things I've done, or the things I've become. Someone who would see me, the real me, and love me anyway." A flicker of sadness crossed her eyes, a glimpse of the loneliness that had haunted her for years. Kate's breath hitched in her throat. Never, in all their bickering and arguments, had she expected this level of honesty from Yelena. This wasn't just about a dream; it was a confession.

    "Yelena…" Kate began, her voice thick with emotion. But the words died in her throat. What could she possibly say that would be a worthy enough answer to that?

    Before Kate could elaborate, Yelena surprised her. The blonde replaced by a sudden urgency, spun Kate around, gripping her forearms with a strength that belied her frame. "You can't walk away," Yelena said, her voice tight with a mixture of desperation and something that sounded suspiciously like fear. "You can't walk away..." Yelena's voice trailed off, her eyes flickering from focusing on one of Kate's eyes and then the other, searching for a flicker of something she hoped would be there.

    Finally, the words tumbled out, raw and unfiltered.

    Kate, catching the blush and the stammer in Yelena's voice, couldn't help but return Sonya's playful grin. "Maybe," the brunette said, a newfound confidence in her voice, "but sometimes blurting things out is exactly what breaks the ice. Right, Yelena?" Her gaze met Yelena’s; a silent challenge wrapped in a playful smile.

    Sonya raised an eyebrow at Kate's boldness. The brunette had certainly come a long way from her flustered entrance just moments ago. A mischievous glint sparked in Sonya's eyes, but before she could add another teasing remark, Melina cleared her throat, the wooden spoon rapping sharply against the pot.

    Melina's gaze flickered between Yelena and Kate, a hint of something unreadable flickered in her eyes, along with something else Kate couldn't quite decipher. Melina then spoke, a barely audible murmur in Russian.

    "Мне нравится этот один."

    Sonya's jaw dropped, a look of pure astonishment plastered on her face. Yelena, for her part, only snorted with a mixture of amusement and exasperation. She rolled her eyes playfully at Kate before turning away, moving to grab a handful of bowls out of a nearby cupboard. The tension in the room had somehow shifted, replaced by a sense of charged anticipation. Kate wasn't sure what Melina's words meant, but one thing was certain: this afternoon hadn’t played out as anticipated.

    That evening, the low hum of conversation and the rhythmic flicker of the fireplace filled the living room. Melina, Yelena, and Sonya were sprawled around a coffee table overflowing with photo albums, the latter’s laughter echoing off the bookshelves. The room exuded a cozy warmth that contrasted sharply with the boisterous entrance that shattered the peace. Melina, perched on the edge of the sofa, meticulously slotted a faded picture back into its place, a faint smile playing on her lips.

    Yelena, sprawled across the other half of the sofa, absently traced the worn leather cover of another album. A contented sigh escaped her lips as she glanced at Kate, curled up in the corner. Kate, nestled between Yelena and the armrest, slept soundly, her brow unfurred, a stray strand of hair tickling Yelena's cheek.

    The quiet scene shattered with a boisterous entrance. The front door slammed open with a bang, and a gust of cold air swept into the room. Alexei, Yelena's father, filled the doorway, his face flushed and his breath coming out in puffs. He stomped the snow off his boots, his booming voice echoing through the room.

    "Unbelievable! Absolutely unbelievable!" he exclaimed, throwing his coat carelessly over a nearby chair. "Those blasted deer – they're a menace, I tell you!"

    Melina, Yelena, and Sonya all looked up, startled by the intrusion. Yelena shot her father a withering look, "Couldn't you have knocked?" she muttered, annoyance lacing her voice. Melina, ever the picture of composure, lowered her teacup and raised an eyebrow. "Alexei, what on earth are you on about now?"

    Alexei, oblivious to the undercurrent of tension, lumbered into the room, shrugging off his coat. "Evening, ladies! Sorry to interrupt your little soiree, but I had to share this outrageous story about these deer..." His voice trailed off again as his gaze fell on the sleeping figure tucked into the corner of the sofa. His eyebrows shot up in surprise. "Yelena? Who is this young lady gracing our living room with her presence?"

    "That is Kate Bishop," Sonya declared, sitting up a little straighter and making the announcement with a flourish.

    Alexei blinked, momentarily confused. "Who?" he rumbled, his brow furrowing slightly. Sonya gasped dramatically, a playful glint in her eyes. "Who?" she echoed, turning to Yelena with mock outrage. "Yelena, how could you not tell your father about Kate? After all this time?"

    Yelena shot Sonya a look that clearly said, "Don't start." Sonya leant back into her slouched position against the cushions, holding up her hands in surrender.

    "There wasn't exactly a formal announcement to make as I understand it, Sonya." Melina teased, obviously herself enough to join in on embarrassing her daughter. Alexei, finally catching on, chuckled heartily. "Ah, I see," he boomed, clapping his hands together. "So, Yelena finally has a secret admirer, eh? Well, come on then, young lady, wake up and say hello to your, shall we say, 'future father-in-law'?"

    He reached out a hand playfully towards Kate, only to be swatted away by Yelena. "Alexei!" the blonde hissed, her voice laced with exasperation. "There is no need to be so dramatic. Kate is a friend if you must know."

    Alexei, ever the observant one, noticed the faint blush creeping up Yelena's neck and the way her gaze kept flickering towards the sleeping Kate. A slow grin spread across his face. He wasn't entirely convinced by Yelena's dismissive explanation, but he decided to play along for now.

    "Ah, a friend," he boomed, his voice laced with amusement. "Well, Yelena, you certainly have good taste in friends. She seems...comfortable," he added, nodding towards Kate. Yelena opened her mouth to retort, but Melina cut her off, a sly smile playing on her lips. "Speaking of comfortable," she interjected, her voice dripping with feigned nonchalance, "did I hear you say something about deer, Alexei?"

    Alexei, ever the eager storyteller, readily jumped on the topic switch. Relief washed over Yelena as she sank back against the sofa, grateful for her mother's intervention. Alexei practically fell into the trap Melina had set, puffing out his chest, a glint of frustration still lingering in his eyes.

    "It turns out deer these days are a particularly wily bunch. Wouldn't stand still for the life of them! Every time I got close, they'd bolt like startled rabbits."

    Sonya snorted with laughter, unable to contain herself. "Oh dear," she said, her voice thick with faux concern. “Perhaps you should take some pointers next time. One of the widows can teach you a thing or two about patience and stealth."

    Alexei bristled at the suggestion. "Patience and stealth?" he scoffed. "Deer hunting is all about precision, timing, and a little bit of luck. Besides, these weren't your average deer. These were practically ninjas in the woods! The point is hunting is a man's sport! It requires skill and cunningness!"

    Melina raised an eyebrow at him. "Oh, really? And here I thought it just involved sitting perfectly still for hours on end, hoping a large, unsuspecting animal wanders by." Alexei sputtered, momentarily speechless. Sonya doubled over with laughter, as Yelena snorted at the expression on her father’s face. "Maybe," Melina suggested, her voice still as sarcastic as it had been, "they were just smarter than you today, Alexei." Alexei scoffed, stopping his pacing to glare mock-seriously at Melina. "Don't be ridiculous, Melina. Those deer were just spooked by something," he added, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, "I think they might have caught wind of my secret weapon." He winked at Yelena, who rolled her eyes playfully. "What secret weapon, Alexei?" she asked, not actually wanting to hear whatever the answer was about to be. Alexei grinned theatrically. "My new camouflage, of course! It's top of the line, practically invisible. Although," he scratched his head thoughtfully, "it might have a slight...floral pattern."

    Yelena groaned. Knowing Alexei, the "floral pattern" was probably a loud, tropical monstrosity that would frighten away any self-respecting deer (and possibly any unsuspecting prey within a five-mile radius).

    Sonya wiping a tear from her eye chimed in, "Oh, please tell me it has those little pink flamingos all over it, Alexei! You know, for maximum stealth.”

    Yelena couldn't help herself. The image that sprang to mind sent Yelena into a fit of giggles. Burying her laughter in the top of Kate's head, she tried to stifle the sound, her shoulders shaking uncontrollably. Kate stirred slightly, mumbling something incoherent before settling back down. A tingled flush spread through her as Kate’s hand instinctively reached up to rest on Yelena's arm.

    “Loud…” Kate mumbled as she pulled herself further into Yelena and away from the arm of the couch.

    Melina watched as Yelena, her laughter finally subsiding, gently guided Kate down. With a soft murmur, Yelena helped Kate shift, so her head rested comfortably in her lap. Kate sighed contentedly, burrowing further into the warmth. Her legs stretched out instinctively, finding a home on the extended L-shaped cushion of the sofa.

    Melina's gaze lingered on the scene. Yelena smoothed the rumpled fabric of Kate's shirt and tucked a stray strand of hair behind her ear. Her touch was light, but undeniably tender. A quiet conversation flowed between Yelena and Sonya, punctuated by gentle laughter. Melina couldn't quite make out the words, but as if on cue, Yelena's fingers found their way to Kate's hair. They brushed through the loose strands with a practiced ease.

    Melina watched the scene unfold with a tenderness in her gaze. It had been a long time since she'd seen her daughter so carefree. The years of training, the weight of their past, it had all etched a seriousness onto Yelena's face that Melina barely recognized anymore. Yelena lifted her head slightly after having ducked it with a shake, at something Sonya had said. The blonde was careful not to disturb Kate's slumber as she twisted slightly to meet Melina's gaze, a silent question hanging in the air. Melina, for once, didn't offer her usual stoic response. Instead, a hint of a smile tugged at the corner of her own lips. "Вы нашли своего знойного радиста.” Melina said simply, her voice quiet but filled with warmth.

    Yelena's heart skipped a beat at her mother's words, a rush of emotion flooding through her. She hadn't expected such an acknowledgment from Melina, but there was a tender acceptance in her mother's eyes that spoke volumes.

    "Gross," Yelena muttered playfully, a small smile tugging at the corners of her lips as she teased her mother. But beneath her light-hearted tone, there was a genuine appreciation for Melina's understanding.

    Melina chuckled softly, her eyes sparkling with amusement. "Yes, yes," she replied with a knowing smile, "but it's clear to see, Yelena. And it's a beautiful thing."

    Chapter 36

    Chapter Notes Hello Hello Hello!

    Sorry chapters are rolling out so slowly, but personal life has been a little nuts so have not had time to sit down and write for quite a while!

    I can feel the mixed reviews for this chapter coming already but hope you enjoy nonetheless!! :/ The fireflies were winking on in the twilight, tiny sparks dancing against the deepening blue of the Ohio evening. Four-year-old Yelena bounced across the backyard, her blonde hair catching the last rays of the setting sun. Laughter bubbled from her lips as she chased a particularly determined bumblebee, her tiny legs pumping in a tireless effort. Inside, the faint glow of the television flickered through the living room window, casting dancing shadows across the lawn. Natasha and Alexei were nestled on the couch, a comfortable silence settling between them as they enjoyed a rare moment of peace. Melina, ever watchful, kept an eye on their little firecracker from the porch steps. Yelena, finally tiring after her energetic exploits, ran back to Melina, a triumphant grin plastered across her face. "Mama! Mama! I almost caught him!" she declared, throwing herself down onto the step with a sigh. Her chest rose and fell with exertion, and a smudge of dirt decorated her otherwise cherubic cheek. Her blonde curls, the colour of summer wheat, stuck to her damp forehead.

    Melina chuckled, reaching down to scoop the little girl into her lap. Wiping the dirt away gently with her thumb, she scanned the darkening field. "He must be very fast, this bumblebee," she said with a wink.

    Yelena nestled into Melina's side, her head resting against her mother's shoulder. Restlessly, she patted a rhythm on Melina's thigh, a silent symphony accompanying the chirping crickets. Contentment washed over her, chasing away the remnants of her earlier frenzy. Just then, a tiny flicker caught Melina's eye – a firefly, its bioluminescence a beacon in the gathering darkness.

    "Look, Yelena," she whispered, pointing towards the dancing light. "See that little star flying around?"

    Yelena's eyes followed Melina's finger, her gaze widening in wonder. The firefly dipped and soared, a tiny spark against the vast expanse of the night sky. A giggle escaped her lips, pure and innocent.

    "It's a firefly," Melina corrected with a smile, brushing a stray curl from Yelena's forehead. "They come out at night to play, just like you."

    Yelena tilted her head, her brow furrowed in concentration. "But where does it go in the daytime?" she asked, her voice hushed with awe.

    Melina wrapped her arm around Yelena, pulling her closer. "They hide away in secret places," she said softly. "Waiting for the sun to go down so they can light up the night again." Yelena let out a yawn that stretched from her toes to her crown. "Firefly," she mumbled, pointing a chubby finger at the tiny creature as it dipped across the horizon line in front of them once more.

    A chuckle escaped Melina's lips. This unadulterated curiosity in her daughter's eyes, it was a treasure. "That's right, sweetheart," Melina said, stroking Yelena's cheek. "A firefly." Suddenly, Yelena's brow furrowed in concentration. "But Mommy," she asked, her voice thick with sleep and genuine confusion, "where's the switch? Like the one on my nightlight. How do they turn off their light?"

    Melina's heart swelled with a love so fierce it almost hurt. This innocent question, a testament to Yelena's untainted worldview, brought a laugh bubbling up from her chest. "There's no switch, Yelena," Melina chuckled, brushing a stray curl from Yelena's forehead. "Fireflies are different. Their light comes from a special kind of magic inside them, a secret power called bioluminescence."

    Yelena's eyes widened. "Biolumines-what?" she slurred, the unfamiliar word a challenge on her sleepy tongue.

    Melina chuckled again. "Think of it like a tiny lantern," she said, trying to simplify it for the little girl. "The firefly has a special chemical inside its body, and when it mixes with another chemical, it makes a glow. Like a little magic lightbulb!"

    Yelena's eyes widened in wonder. "Magic lightbulb?" she echoed, her tiredness momentarily forgotten.

    "Exactly!" Melina said, her voice filled with amusement. "Just like our fireflies here, some creatures have their own special way of making light."

    Yelena pondered this for a moment, her gaze fixed on another firefly flitting past them. Then, a mischievous glint sparked in her eyes. "Do you think I could have a magic lightbulb inside me too, Mama?" she asked, a hopeful lilt in her voice.

    Melina's heart clenched at her daughter's innocent question. In a perfect world, Yelena's light would shine brightly, unhindered. But the truth, the darkness that awaited them, loomed large in her mind.

    Taking a deep breath, Melina forced a smile. "Maybe not exactly like a firefly," she said gently, "but you have your own kind of special light, Yelena. A bright smile that can light up a room, and a kind heart that can warm anyone's day."

    Yelena considered this, a thoughtful frown creasing her forehead. Then, a smile, genuine and wide, spread across her face. "My own special light," she repeated, the words a soft melody in the twilight air.

    Melina wrapped her arms tighter around her daughter, the fireflies twinkling like distant stars above them. In that moment, bathed in the soft glow of the Ohio night, Melina held onto the fragile hope that Yelena's inner light would forever defy the darkness that threatened to consume them.

    A sigh escaped Yelena's lips, a blissful content settling over her features. "Mama," she mumbled, gazing up at the fireflies with a touch of sadness in her voice, "can they stay forever?"

    Melina's heart ached at the unspoken fear behind Yelena's question. The impermanence of things, the fear of losing something precious - these were concepts Melina desperately wanted to shield her daughter from for as long as possible. Being torn away from something you love is the worst pain imaginable, Melina would know.

    "Fireflies, like us, need their rest too, little one," Melina explained gently. "Just like you get sleepy after a long day of playing, fireflies need to sleep to have enough energy to shine their light again tomorrow."

    Yelena's brow furrowed in concentration. "But… they're so pretty," she protested, her voice barely a whisper. "Can't they just stay awake a little longer?"

    Melina smiled understandingly. "I know, sweetheart," she said, brushing a kiss against Yelena's forehead. "But everything needs sleep, even fireflies. They'll be back tomorrow night, lighting up the garden just for us."

    Yelena pondered this for a moment, a flicker of disappointment lingering in her eyes. Then, a new idea struck her. "Can I sleep outside with them, Mama?" she asked, her voice filled with hopeful anticipation. "Then I can watch them all night long!"

    Melina chuckled, the sound warm and comforting. "As much as I love the idea, little one, sleeping outside all night wouldn't be very comfortable.”

    Yelena looked up at Melina, her eyes wide and pleading. "But Mama…"

    Melina knew that look. The look that meant negotiation was futile. Instead, she offered a compromise.

    "Tell you what," she said, her voice soft but firm. "How about I hold you right here until you fall asleep? And then once you are away with the fairies, I’ll carry you up to bed?” Yelena's shoulders slumped slightly, but a small smile tugged at the corners of her lips. The idea of being held by her mother and watching the fireflies was a close second to sleeping amongst them.

    "Fairies?" she echoed, a spark of amusement dancing in her eyes.

    Melina winked. "Of course," she said, her voice playful. "Fireflies are just fairies in disguise. They sprinkle their magic dust all over the garden at night, making everything glow." Yelena giggled, the sound like wind chimes in the warm summer air. She wriggled around in Melina's arms until she found the perfect spot, her head nestled comfortably against her mother's chest. Her gaze, however, remained fixed on the fireflies, their tiny lights flitting through the deepening twilight.

    For a while, the only sound was the rhythmic chirping of crickets and Yelena's soft breaths. Her eyelids fluttered closed for a moment, then snapped open again, captivated by the firefly ballet. Melina, her heart overflowing with a bittersweet love, traced gentle circles on Yelena's forehead with her thumb. The small girl’s breaths grew shallow, even, and a peaceful smile graced her lips.

    Melina held her daughter close, a silent tear tracing a path down her cheek. This moment, this fragile normalcy, was a treasure she would forever hold onto in her memory. As Yelena drifted off to sleep, Melina knew, with a heavy heart, that this wouldn't last forever. The Red Room loomed large in their future, a dark cloud threatening to extinguish the innocent light of her little firefly.

    But for now, in the quiet embrace of the Ohio night, Melina clung to the hope that she could delay the inevitable. She would be Yelena's shield, her protector, for as long as she could. She would fight with every fibre of her being to keep her daughter's inner light burning bright, even in the face of the coming darkness.

    The morning air was a crisp bite, clinging to their faces and turning exhaled breaths into frosty clouds. The ground crunched beneath their boots, a thin layer of ice making the farmyard a treacherous ballet. Sunlight, pale and tentative, peeked over the horizon, casting long shadows from the skeletal trees bordering the fields.

    Melina tossed a hefty scoop of mash into the trough, the pigs erupting in a symphony of snorts and shoves. Melina hoisted the heavy bucket of slops, its contents sloshing precariously, while Yelena trailed behind, her breath puffing out in white clouds. Reaching the pigsty, the squeals of the hungry animals rose to greet them. Melina unlatched the wooden gate, a chorus of eager snorts erupting from within. The mother pig, a hulking mass of pink flesh, emerged first, nudging past Yelena with surprising force. A gaggle of piglets, clumsy on their short legs, tumbled after her, their pink snouts rooting for scraps in the snow. For a time, there was just the rhythmic sloshing of slop and the contented grunts of the pigs. Melina stole a glance at Yelena, who was watching a gaggle of piglets huddle around their mother, jostling for a prime spot at her udder. A soft smile played on Yelena's lips. It softened the sharp angles of her face, making her look younger, lighter. Melina's chest ached with a bittersweet pang.

    The image before her – the fierce protectiveness of the mother pig, the playful squabbling of the piglets, the quiet understanding between them – mirrored, in a way, their own dynamic. But unlike the piglets who would eventually leave their mother's side, Yelena had never known the comfort of a true mother's love.

    Melina's gaze drifted back to Yelena, who had bent down to scratch one of the piglets behind the ears. The gentleness of the gesture, so unlike Yelena's usual brusqueness, tore at the dam Melina had built around her secret for so long.

    A silent debate raged within her. Should she tell Yelena? The truth, the one Melina had buried deep within herself for all these years, the truth that would change everything between them. The truth that Yelena wasn't just a job, a chore, a widow, but her own flesh and blood. Melina gripped the handle of the slop bucket, her knuckles white. The weight of the truth felt heavier than ever, a truth that could either tear them apart or bind them closer than ever before.

    Yelena, finally finished with her portion of the slop, straightened, and brushed her gloved hands on her coat. Her gaze fell on Melina, and a furrow appeared between her brows. The stark white of Melina's knuckles, straining against the worn wood, didn't escape her notice. “Ok. Out with it, Melina.” Yelena's voice was firm, laced with a hint of exasperation. The vague answers and dodging tactics were wearing thin.

    Melina's gaze darted around the pigsty, landing on the oblivious animals. Their grunts and snuffles filled the air, a constant, mindless background noise. But in her head, the silence roared, a deafening cacophony of what-ifs and maybes.

    Stealing a glance at Yelena, Melina saw a flicker of something new in her eyes, a vulnerability masked by concern. It was a small spark, but it ignited a desperate hope within her.

    Maybe.

    Maybe Yelena, beneath the hardened exterior, wouldn't reject her.

    Maybe, just maybe, there was a chance for understanding, for a bond deeper than they had ever known.

    Melina drew in a shaky breath, the frigid air stinging her lungs. With a trembling hand, she reached into her pocket and retrieved a faded photograph.

    This was it.

    Yelena's brow furrowed further, her gaze flitting between Melina's trembling hand and her own weathered face. Curiosity, tinged with a hint of apprehension, flickered in her eyes. Slowly, cautiously, she reached out and took the photograph.

    The image, muted by age and countless viewings, depicted a scene both ordinary and extraordinary. A woman, her face obscured by time and the angle of the photo, cradled a baby in her arms. The baby, swaddled in a simple cloth, looked up with wide, curious eyes. The photo itself wasn't particularly remarkable, but the weight it carried in Melina's hand was immense.

    Yelena turned the photo over, her fingers tracing the smooth, worn surface. A flicker of surprise crossed her face as she spotted faded ink on the back. Squinting, she could just make out an inscription: Yelena V. Belova Her breath hitched in her throat. This was her name, but why was it written on this photo of a baby she didn't recognize? She looked back up at Melina, her heart pounding a frantic rhythm against her ribs. "What is this?" she asked, her voice barely a whisper, a tremor echoing the one in Melina's hand.

    Melina, her face pale and drawn, met Yelena's gaze. The secret, held captive for so long, seemed to thrum in the air between them. She didn't answer Yelena's question directly, but her voice, when she finally spoke, held a quiet desperation.

    "The V stands for Vostokoff," Melina began, her words measured. "Your real name, Yelena, is Елена Востокофф Белова.”

    Yelena stared at the photo, the inscription blurring before her eyes. A strange, disorienting wave of dizziness washed over her. "Yelena Vostokoff Belova?" she echoed, the name sounding alien on her tongue. It was as if someone had ripped open a part of her, she never knew existed.

    Anger, sharp and sudden, flared in her chest. Years of conditioning, of being a nameless cog in the Red Room machine, warred with this new, unsettling truth. She slammed her free hand down on the wooden trough with a force that sent a startled squawk erupting from the nearest pig.

    "Explain this!" the blonde shouted, "What is this photo? Who is that baby? Why does it have my name on it?” The fury in Yelena's voice was a whip, cracking across the frosty air. "It's you, Yelena," Melina stammered, her voice barely audible over the pounding in her chest. "The baby in the picture... it's you."

    Yelena scoffed, the sound harsh and disbelieving. "Me? How can it be me? I don't remember anything like this. I don't remember any parents! They’re dead."

    Melina's heart ached at the raw pain in Yelena's voice. Taking a steadying breath, she forced herself to meet Yelena's gaze. "There's a reason for that, Yelena. A reason I haven't been able to tell you." Then, with a voice thick with emotion, she added, "Belova was my mother's maiden name."

    The name hung in the air, a foreign sound to Yelena's ears yet somehow familiar. A flicker of recognition, faint and fleeting, sparked in her eyes. "Your mother's…"

    Melina pressed on, "And Vostokoff was my father's."

    Yelena stared at the photo, the inscription blurring with the sting of tears welling up in her eyes. Yet, the weight of Melina's words, the tremor in her voice, held a truth she couldn't ignore.

    "But why?" she finally choked out, her voice tight. "Why is my name written on this photo? Why is it connected to you and your family?"

    Yelena's mind reeled. A father? A mother? These were concepts she'd only encountered in stolen glances at dusty storybooks, fragments of a past deliberately shattered by the Red Room. Now, Melina was claiming to be a part of that past, a connection she had no memory of. The anger flared anew, hotter than before, but this time laced with a tremor of fear. Melina reached out, a hesitant hand hovering near Yelena's arm. Yelena flinched, a conditioned response to any sudden movement. But Melina held her ground, her eyes pleading for understanding. "Because, Yelena," she said softly, "that baby in the picture… that's you."

    The world seemed to tilt on its axis for Yelena. The faded photograph, clutched tightly in her trembling hand, suddenly held an impossible truth. Denial, a reflex honed by years of manipulation, rose like a shield.

    "No," she spat, the word a sharp denial that echoed in the stillness of the morning. "That's impossible. I don't remember… I can't…" Her voice trailed off, choked by a rising tide of emotion. The photo, once a mere curiosity, now burned in her hand, a searing indictment of a fabricated past.

    "How do you have this?" Yelena finally managed, her voice hoarse.

    Melina's hand tightened around the other one, her knuckles white. "I've had it… since the day it was taken," she confessed, her voice thick with emotion. "You were about three months old in that picture. It was the last day I ever saw you… until they assigned us both to the Ohio mission when you were three years old."

    "Three months..." she repeated, the words hanging heavy in the air. "But... I don't remember anything before the Red Room."

    Melina's eyes welled up again, a heartbreaking mix of sorrow and resolve. "They took you, Yelena," she said, her voice thick with emotion. "But you would not remember anything that young. No. Brain too little.”

    The explanation, spoken in a way that tugged at something deep within Yelena, sent shivers down her spine. Yet, logic warred with the strange warmth spreading in her chest. A scoff escaped Yelena's lips. "This is ridiculous. We were orphans, Melina. Expendable assets for Dreykov. Sonya is right, you’ve lost it."

    How dare Melina play these mind games with her after all these years? But even as Yelena turned to storm away, Melina's next words snagged her attention.

    "Orphan," Melina repeated, the word laced with a bitterness that mirrored Yelena's own. "That's what they told you, isn't it? But it's a lie. A cruel lie they use to control you." Yelena stopped, her back stiff. Control. It was the very essence of the Red Room, the weaponization of their identities.

    Melina stepped closer, her voice dropping to a low, urgent whisper. "I fell pregnant, Yelena. It was unexpected, a miracle even, before my fourth cycle of processing. I felt rebellious whilst out on a mission and well, you can guess the rest. Dreykov…" she faltered, a flicker of fear crossing her face, "he always had had a strange fondness for me. He allowed me to keep the pregnancy. But after you were born, after my recovery…" Her voice trailed off, the silence heavy with unspoken pain.

    Yelena's breath hitched.

    "After I was born?" Yelena rasped, the words catching in her throat like shards of glass. It was a question, but it also hung in the air as a horrifying accusation. Melina met her gaze, "They took you from me, Yelena. When you were just three months old. I was cycled through the Red Room for a fourth time. They called it a necessary precaution. It was… Dreykov's way. He said it would make me ‘pure’ again, free from emotional attachments."

    Yelena felt a coldness creep through her veins, a stark contrast to the burning knot of anger in her stomach. "So, what?" she spat, her voice laced with a bitter mockery. "You're just another cog in the machine, another disposable asset who happened to lay an egg? Is that it?" Melina flinched, the pain in her eyes deepening. "No, Yelena. No, that's not it at all." Her voice trembled, raw and desperate. "I… I loved you. From the moment I held you in my arms, I knew…" She trailed off, unable to finish the sentence, the weight of her unspoken love hanging heavy between them.

    Yelena stared, her mind reeling. Love? The concept was as foreign to her as the name "Belova” now seemed. Her entire life had been built on the foundation of her being an orphan, a weapon. Yet, here stood Melina, claiming not only to be her mother but to have loved her. It was too much, a truth that threatened to shatter the very core of her being. "Melina," she finally forced out, her voice barely a whisper. "Say it. Please. I just need to hear you say it."

    Melina took a shuddering breath, her shoulders slumping under the weight of the secret. There was so much she wanted to explain, so much context before the devastating truth. But the urgency in Yelena's voice brooked no delay. Melina saw the raw vulnerability in Yelena's eyes, the desperate need for confirmation. She understood.

    Taking a deep breath, Melina steeled herself. This was it. The moment of truth, the culmination of years of silence and yearning.

    But before the words could leave her lips, a strange urge took hold of her. A need to explain, to bridge the vast chasm between their fabricated past and this newfound reality. "Yelena," she began, her voice trembling slightly, "your name… it wasn't chosen at random. It means something.”

    Clint, leaned back in his chair, stretching his arms above his head with a tired groan. "Maybe Laura's right. We're looking at Fisk from the top down, trying to crack a fortress. Maybe we need to find a way in from the side."

    Natasha, intrigued, raised an eyebrow. "What do you mean?"

    Clint gave a wry smile. "Everyone comes from somewhere, right? Every empire has a foundation. Maybe if we dig into Fisk's past, into the people who helped him build his little kingdom, we might find a weakness. Someone with a grudge, someone with something to lose."

    Laura, her eyes still glued to the screen, perked up. "Exactly! People leave trails, Clint. Even the most careful ones. Financial records, old associates, buried scandals – there has to be something we can use as leverage."

    A flicker of excitement sparked in Natasha's eyes. "I like it. We can use SHIELD's resources to dig into Fisk's past, see who he used to climb his way to the top. Maybe someone got pushed aside, left empty-handed. Someone with a bone to pick and a story to tell." Clint nodded, a grin spreading across his face. "And while you two dig in the dirt, I can use my contacts on the street level. See if anyone remembers Fisk before he was Kingpin, anyone with a grudge or a story they've been keeping buried."

    “No. That’s it.” Laura said, her head snapping up from her screen, “See if anyone remembers Fisk before he was Kingpin. That’s it.”

    “Laura?” Clint asked cautiously.

    “What happened to his family? Parents? Siblings? Grandparents?”

    “Fisk…” Nat paused as she flicked to the front page of the file in front of her, “he's an only child. His grandparents are deceased, as are his parents."

    “Right. That’s what I thought.”

    “What do you mean?”

    “It’s too clean. Think about it. Fisk built his empire from the ground up. He clawed his way to the top, made enemies along the way. Wouldn't someone, somewhere, remember a family member? An aunt, an uncle, a disgruntled cousin? The fact that there's nothing – no mention of any extended family whatsoever – it's too clean."

    Clint began to see the logic in Laura's argument. "You think there's something Fisk is hiding? A family secret maybe? Something that could be used against him?"

    Nat nodded her understanding, “So, if we can find a relative, someone who knew Fisk before the power and the money, someone who might have a grudge or a hidden truth – that could be our leverage?"

    Laura shook her head at the pair of Avengers in front of her, smiling to herself at their point- blank thinking. “No.”

    “That is legit what you just said.” Clint groaned, his exasperation making Laura only smiler wider.

    “I’m saying… any living relatives don’t matter. People say that dead men tell no tales… except when they do…” Laura raised an eyebrow as she spun her laptop around, the screen pulled up on a digital file of Kingpin’s parents death certificates. “His mother’s checks out. Old age. We know she remarried twice and then spent the end of her life in a care home. We have the records for that.”

    “And his father’s?” Natasha leaned closer, scrutinizing the document.

    “Declaration of Presumed Death.” Laura declared, a triumphant grin spreading across her face.

    Natasha furrowed her brow, leaning closer to the screen. "Presumed death? But that means…"

    "His body was never found," Laura finished, her voice laced with a newfound excitement. "No accident report, no police investigation, no record of a burial. Just a court order declaring him legally dead after four years of being missing."

    Clint whistled, a low, impressed sound. "That's one hell of a secret to keep buried. A missing father, presumed dead, and then suddenly young Fisk is rolling in dough. The plot thickens, wouldn't you say?"

    Laura nodded vigorously, her fingers flying across the keyboard. "Exactly! There has to be more to this story. Why would a man just vanish? And why would his son wait four years before declaring him dead? There's something we don’t know."

    Natasha raised a cautionary hand. "Hold on a second. Declarations of presumed death are usually used when there's no body and no hope of finding one. It's a legal way to settle someone's affairs, not some elaborate cover-up."

    Laura didn't back down, her eyes gleaming with determination. "Maybe in most cases, Nat. But Fisk isn't most people. He's built his empire on secrets and lies. And a missing father, presumed dead, with no explanation – that screams suspicious to me."

    "Laura's right. We need to dig deeper. Find out everything we can about this disappearance. Was there any foul play suspected? Did the police have any leads they never followed up on? Maybe someone out there remembers something, a detail the authorities missed." Natasha, however, wasn't convinced. She chewed on her bottom lip, worry etched on her face. "Clint," she began cautiously, "Bill Fisk was a politician. He ran for Third District Council of New York City. There could have been so many people out for his head. Political rivals, disgruntled constituents… we could follow this trail for weeks, chase down every lead, and come up with absolutely nothing. It could be a complete dead end, a waste of precious time."

    Clint sighed, running a hand through his hair. He understood Natasha's concern. Fisk was a master manipulator, the kind of man who could leave a trail of false leads and dead ends in his wake.

    "Look, Nat," he said, his voice softening, "I know it's a risk. But right now, it's the best lead we have, the only thread we can pull on to try and understand Fisk, to find a weakness. We can't just sit here and wait for him to make his next move."

    A wry smile flickered across Clint's lips. "Besides," he continued, a hint of teasing in his voice, "if all else fails, maybe we can consult our resident expert. You know, the one who seems to have an uncanny knack for uncovering secrets, even the most deeply buried ones." Natasha's eyes narrowed playfully. "You wouldn't dare," she warned, a ghost of a smile battling with the worry lines on her face. “We are meant to be letting her enjoy her holiday with her girlfriend.”

    "Dare what?" Clint feigned innocence, raising his eyebrows in mock surprise. "Ask Yelena for a little help? Honestly, with the way she was spewing out information back at the Compound, I wouldn't be surprised if she already knows everything about Kingpin's past, childhood teddy bear collection and all."

    Natasha's smile widened, the tension evaporating as Clint's teasing broke the ice. "Alright, alright," she conceded, shaking her head in amusement. "Yelena does have a knack for finding things out and for keeping said things to herself apparently.” The redhead pauses, “We don’t have to ask Yelena.”

    “Eh?” Clint’s brow furrowed in thought.

    “She’s not the only widow we have access to.” Nat spoke, a sly grin spreading across her face.

    “Sonya?” Laura questioned with a newfound spark of interest in the conversation. “Everything Yelena knows, it's a safe bet that Sonya does too. And with her network of ex- Widows scattered around the globe, she might be able to dig up something on Bill Fisk that even SHIELD's archives missed."

    Clint, however, scratched his head thoughtfully, "Hold on a sec. Didn't Yelena mention something about Sonya and the other Widows being off-limits?”

    Natasha smirked. "True, Yelena did say that. But," she continued, a glint in her eye, "she also freed them to make their own choices. If we approach Sonya and explain the situation, if she wants to help, who are we to deny her that choice?"

    Clint chuckled, a low rumble escaping his throat. “This idea of finding loopholes in your sister’s words might amuse you now Nat, but Yelena… well, let's just say she's not exactly known for her sense of... forgiveness. If she finds out, we went behind her back and recruited her best friend…"

    He trailed off, leaving the unspoken threat hanging in the air. The image of Yelena, arms crossed and a steely glint in her eyes, was enough to send a shiver down Clint's spine. “I’ll handle it,” Nat waved the unspoken threat off nonchalantly, before she paused, “Or… Kate will.” The redhead’s smirk returned as the couple of the house snorted.
